Come with Me to the Festival

On Thursday the Haifa Film Festival will open • A house correspondent recommends a few films to be screened there

The 30th edition of the Haifa Film Festival, opening this coming Thursday with a screening of "The Judge," starring Robert Downey Jr. and Robert Duvall, offers this year a long and almost exaggerated array of fascinating and recommended films.

Want more updates? Join Israel Today on Facebook

Besides an intriguing Israeli competition featuring, among others, "A Good Death" by Sharon Maymon and Tal Granit, "Jonah" by Nir Bergman, "You to Me at Night" by Assaf Korman, and "Manpower" by Noam Kaplan, and besides a visit by the excellent Russian director Andrei Zvyagintsev ("The Return," "The Banishment"), who will present his acclaimed new film "Leviathan," the festival will also screen some of the most talked-about works of the past year, such as "Winter Sleep" by Nuri Bilge Ceylan ("Once Upon a Time in Anatolia"), which won the Palme d'Or at the recent Cannes Festival, and the American "Whiplash," which won the grand prize at the Sundance Festival.

To make it easier for you to navigate the rich program, here are a few more films, somewhat less known, that are definitely worth being aware of.

• "20,000 Days on Earth": Singer-poet-writer-screenwriter Nick Cave has disappeared somewhat in recent years, but this thrilling, stylish and inspiring musical biography, which stands somewhere between an artistic documentary and a self-portrait, is sure to delight and move anyone who has been captivated by his unique charm over the years. Directors Ian Forsyth and Jane Pollard take Cave on a journey to the past, send him to sift through archive photos, introduce him to prominent figures he collaborated with (such as Björk Guðmundsdóttir and Kylie Minogue) and accompany him as he works on his new album. Cave, who turned 57 this year, opens up to the camera, reveals fascinating details about his creative process, philosophizes as if there were no tomorrow, and of course, also sings. A huge film about a huge artist.

• "Ida": After several decades of working in England, Polish director Paweł Pawlikowski returns to his homeland to present a stunning black-and-white drama set in the early 1960s. At the center of the plot stands a young and innocent nun who sets out with her Jewish (and communist) aunt on a roots journey in search of her family who were murdered during the Nazi occupation. Through stunning monochromatic cinematography and superb performances by the two women, Pawlikowski creates a tight and precise film containing enormous amounts of sorrow and guilt. "Ida" arrives in Haifa after garnering praise at countless festivals and after being earmarked as a leading candidate for winning the Best Foreign Film Oscar at the upcoming ceremony. In its case, the hype is completely justified.

• "Like Cattle": British director David Mackenzie ("Spread," "Perfect Sense") may not be particularly consistent, but his new film is undoubtedly one of his best. It's a visceral, violent and unexpected prison drama that follows Eric (Jake O'Connell), an angry young prisoner who is placed in a detention facility meant for adult inmates. The fact that his father (Ben Mendelsohn), whom he hasn't seen since he was five, is also imprisoned there, is supposed to help him survive, but in reality only makes things more complicated and dangerous. O'Connell (expected to become a star following his appearance here) and Mendelsohn ("Killing Them Softly") simply set the screen on fire, and Mackenzie manages to make the charged relationship that develops between them complex, extraordinary and unforgettable.

• "Clouds of Sils Maria": French director Olivier Assayas ("Irma Vep," "Summer Hours," "Carlos") is also not known for consistency, but as in Mackenzie's case, he too is at peak form in his new film. Juliette Binoche plays an aging film star, Kristen Stewart plays her personal assistant, and Assayas uses both of them to delicately and mockingly probe the creative process, performance, aging and female jealousy. Binoche delivers one of her best performances in recent years. The excellent Stewart proves there is life after "Twilight," and Chloë Grace Moretz ("Kick-Ass"), who appears in a guest role, also manages to leave her mark. The result is elegant, enigmatic and thought-provoking, and if you wish, you can see it as the feminine version of "Molière on a Bicycle."

• "Killer Joe": Michael C. Hall ("Dexter"), Sam Shepard and Don Johnson star in a dark and trashy Texas thriller from horror director Jim Mickle (responsible for the American remake of the Mexican cannibal film "We Are What We Are"). A law-abiding family man kills a burglar who broke into his home and finds himself swept into a violent and chilling maelstrom involving corrupt cops, gangsters and snuff films. On paper you've already seen this film before, but Mickle and his regular screenwriter Nick Damici navigate the work in surprising directions. The three leads gleefully commit themselves to the apparently inferior material, and genre fans are sure to leave the theater with a sickly smile.

• "Corn Island": The big winner at the Karlovy Vary Festival is a film festival par excellence. It takes place entirely on a small island in the Mtkvari River that separates Georgia from Abkhazia, has almost no dialogue, and most of its minutes are devoted to methodically following an old man and his granddaughter engaged in agricultural work. Yet if you fancy diving into a fascinating and very special cinematic experience, and you are blessed with a bit more patience than average, "Corn Island" by Giorgi Ovsiannikov, which tells a simple parable about man, nature and eternal political conflicts, is undoubtedly the film for you.

• "Truffaut Forever": Alongside some of the greatest works of legendary French director François Truffaut ("Two English Girls," "Jules and Jim" and "The 400 Blows"), to be screened at the festival marking 30 years since his death, this new documentary, directed by Alexandre Moua, will also be screened. You won't find earth-shattering revelations here, but through old interviews with the great director, perusal of his personal letters and conversations with his friends and colleagues, Moua's delicate, modest and not very long work sketches a moving human portrait of a great filmmaker and awakens a strong desire to watch again the splendid body of his work.

"יצא לי לשמוע שירים ישנים יותר, למשל דנה אינטרנשיונל מהאירוויזיון. אני אוהבת את המוזיקה שלה אבל זה סגנון ישן קצת. אני גם מאוד אוהבת את נטע ברזילי. אני מתה על התרבות הישראלית, את היהדות, כל מה שקשור לזה". אור בתקופות חשוכות כאמור, אליעד לא היה היחיד להגיב על הקאבר בעברית. הסרטון בעל התפאורה והאפקטים המושקעים, שתוך מספר ימים צבר כ-150 אלף צפיות, קיבל כמעט פי שניים סימוני "אנלייק" לעומת "לייק" ותגובות רבות שנעות בין זעם לבין הטחת עלבונות. כאמור, אין זו הפעם הראשונה שסרטוניה שנויים במחלוקת. כשהיא נשאלת על הסיבות שלדעתה גרמו לצופים להגיב ברשעות כלפיה, ועל כך שנראה שהמגמה שבה סרטוניה מקבלים יותר "אנלייקים" מ"לייקים" נמשכת כבר תקופה ארוכה, היא טוענת שאינה יודעת למה, אבל מסבירה שלדעתה אנשים נתלים במי שהיתה בעבר – ולא רוצים לראות אותה משתנה. "הייתה לי המון שנאה בלב, אבל השתניתי, ואנשים לא מוכנים לקבל את זה", היא אומרת. "מבחינתי זה בסדר, אני תמיד מוצאת אור בתקופות חשוכות, ויכולה להוות עדות חיה למישהי שהשתנתה בגדול. כשהתחלתי לקבל את כל השנאה הזאת כלפיי הבנתי שאני צריכה לשנות את עצמי ולהפוך לחיובית, ועכשיו אני עושה מדיטציה, בוחרת להרגיש טוב ומרגישה טוב". "אני לא מבינה יותר מדי את הקונפליקט, אבל מאז שאני עם מוזס ואנחנו מדברים על ישראל אנשים ממש מתעצבנים מזה" אם פייטס באמת אינה יודעת מה גרם לגלי השנאה כלפיה, או שמא היא מעדיפה להצניע את הסיבות, קשה לומר, כי שערוריות היו מנת חלקה תקופה ארוכה. בין היתר היא הכריזה שהיא מזדהה כטרנסג'נדרית ומרגישה כגבר הומוסקסואל כי היא "נמשכת לגברים גאים ואוהבת גלאם וזוהר"; שאינה מזדהה עוד כבן אדם; ביקשה שישתמשו בכינוי גוף רבים כשמדברים עליה; עשתה שימוש בבלאקפייס. היא גם הכריזה שיש לה הפרעת זהות, והודתה שיש לה צורך קבוע בתשומת לב. בריאיון ל"ביזנס אינסיידר" היא חשפה שחלק מהסרטונים היותר הזויים שלה הועלו "רק כדי לקבל צפיות", וכן הודתה שהיא לפעמים מציגה את עצמה כ"מטומטמת יותר ממה שהיא באמת", כי לדבריה אנשים לא היו צופים בה אם הייתה נאמנה לעצמה ולמי שהיא. אבל יאמרו מה שיגידו עליה, ותגיד היא בעצמה מה שתרצה, יש דברים שאי אפשר לקחת לה, ובהם ההספק מעורר הפליאה שלה בנבכיי תעשיית הבידור העולמית. פייטס הוציאה 11 ספרים (ששמותיהם, בתרגום חופשי, נעים בין "ההיסטוריה של אי השפיות שלי" ל"101 שירים על האקס שלי"), סדרת מוצרי טיפוח לפנים (שהתקבלה בתגובות מעורבות) והספיקה לתעד את חייה המלאים, כולל אהבות, פרידות, סכסוכים, בינג'ים ובכי על רצפת המטבח באינספור סרטונים, כשהכל ארוז בתוך אישיות עליזה, זוהרת, מצחקקת ובעלת רצון טוב, שלא תמיד מתממש. אוהבת בחורים יהודים את מוזס, ארוסה הישראלי בן ה-44, הכירה פייטס דרך אחותו, הילה, שנשואה ליוטיובר המצליח איתן קליין, כוכב רשת בזכות עצמו שמפיק פודקאסטים שזוכים למיליוני צפיות. "השתתפתי בפודקאסט שלהם ותוך כדי כך התחיל סגר הקורונה, שבגללו האח מוזס לא יכול היה להגיע", משחזרת פייטס. "הם סיפרו לי עליו כי הם ידעו שהוא הטייפ שלי – אני אוהבת בחורים יהודים – ואז החלטנו לעשות את הסגר ביחד, הוא ואני, ותשעה חודשים אחרי שהתחלנו לצאת – התארסנו". מוזס, שנוכח ברבים מאוד מסרטוניה, נראה בדיוק ההפך הגמור מפייטס – רגוע, שקט ושליו. "הוא לא מתעצבן אף פעם וזה מה שעוזר לי להירגע", היא צוחקת. חוגגת את ראש השנה. טרישה פייטס היה לך קשר לישראל או ליהדות לפני כן? "תמיד נמשכתי לתרבות הזאת ויצאתי עם יהודים, אבל גם אם הם היו מאוד בעניין הם לא רצו להתחתן איתי כי לא הייתי יהודייה, או שלא לקחו אותי ברצינות כשאמרתי שאני מוכנה להתגייר. עם מוזס זה בכלל לא היווה עניין לדיון, הוא אמר לי שאני בכלל לא חייבת להתגייר. בעיניי יהודים הם בני זוג יותר מכבדים". את עדיין חושבת להתגייר? "תכננתי להתגייר אבל אני לא יודעת אם אספיק לפני החתונה. אנחנו רוצים להגיע לארץ בפברואר או במרץ. מוזס לא ממש דתי, אני מנסה לשמור כשרות בהרבה מקרים אבל לו זה פחות משנה. אפילו רציתי לצום ביום כיפור, והוא אמר שלא צריך ושכבר כילד הוא לא היה צם. אבל אמא שלו שומרת כשרות, ואני אוהבת את הקונספט הזה". ראיתי שהעלית כמה סרטונים שאת מקיימת בהם סדר פסח וראש השנה. "יצאתי עם יהודים אמריקנים והם לא לימדו אותי שום דבר על החגים. ראש השנה הקודם היה הראשון שלי והייתי ממש נלהבת לחגוג אותו. אנשים לא מדברים מספיק על החגים היהודיים, על מה אומרת צלחת הסדר, מבחינתי זה יותר מגניב מחג הפסחא כי זה תנכ"י". חוגגת את ליל הסדר. טרישה פייטס כשהתארסה, קיבלה לא מעט תגובות קשות בעקבות הקשר עם הבחור הישראלי. "הייתי רוצה לעבור לישראל לפחות לשנה, אבל מוזס עוד לא סגור על זה. בכללי אין לנו תוכניות כרגע. זו פעם ראשונה שלי שאהיה בארץ, למרות שאבא שלי היה בישראל כמה פעמים כשעשה טיולים עם הכנסייה הקתולית. אני מאוד אוהבת את יפו ורוצה להתחתן שם". הצד של אליעד אליעד נחום לא הכיר את טרישה פייטס לפני כן – לא היכרות אמיתית, בכל אופן, אלא רק דרך טיקטוק. "כל שיר שהעליתי בעברית לטיקטוק זכה לדואט ממנה", הוא מספר. "היא כתבה לי שחבר שלה ישראלי וככה היא לומדת עברית. זה נחמד, אבל לא ציפיתי בכלל להפקה המטורפת של הקליפ הזה. ממש הופתעתי כשראיתי את הצילום והתחפושת המושקעת של היצור הימי בקליפ". הגיעו אליך תגובות מחו"ל? "בעיניי זה מאוד אמיץ להעלות שיר בעברית לערוץ עם מיליוני מנויים שכולם דוברי אנגלית, ועוד קליפ מושקע כל כך, שכששלחתי אותו לאנשים הם שאלו אם היא לקחה סצנות מסרט בכיכובה והדביקה על השיר. זה ריגש אותי, זה היווה עבורי מין אישור כזה, כי הרבה אומרים לי בארץ שאני שר טוב באנגלית והמוזיקה שלי יכולה לעבוד גם בחו"ל. עשיתי עכשיו דואט עם זמר אמריקני בשם רוטימי, וזו פעם ראשונה שאמן ישראלי מתארח באלבום אמריקני, לרוב זה הפוך". ראיתי תגובות שהציעו ששם השיר היה מיתרגם יותר טוב ל"your inner peace" מאשר "your silence", שנשמע כמו "השתיקה שלך". "התלבטתי בשאלה איך לקרוא לו באנגלית, אבל היה נראה לי שגם במשמעות של 'השתיקה שלך' זה מתאים. הוא נכתב בתקופת סגר הקורונה, והוא מין שיר עידוד לי ולחברה שלי. היינו תקועים בבית בחוסר מעש וכל הזמן אמרתי לה 'הכל יעבור, זו רק תקופה, אני איתך'. זה הכניס אותנו לדאון. פתאום אין הופעות, אין עבודה. מזל שהתקופה הזו חלפה".

# "I'm Dying For Israeli Culture": Interview with American YouTube Star Who Covered Elyad

Trisha Paytas is a name familiar to most Americans, and soon apparently to many Israelis too. With millions of followers on social media, controversial videos and an Israeli fiancé, she gives her first interview to Israel Today and talks about her love of Judaism, the harsh reactions she receives, and the impressive clip with a Hebrew performance of Elyad's "Your Silence"

And a surprise: which Big Brother contestant does she admire?

When you add up her followers across various social media platforms, you get a number that far exceeds Israel's population. This doesn't bother American YouTube star Trisha Paytas, who goes crazy over our local version of Big Brother. "I follow Big Brother Israel on Instagram and I'm dying over your version," says Paytas, who boasts 5.4 million followers on her YouTube channel alone ("blndsundoll4mj") and another 6.4 million followers on her TikTok channel. "I can only see short clips uploaded to YouTube from the show, but it's way more interesting than the American or British version."

Would you like to participate in the Israeli version of the reality show? "I would die for that! I'm ready to learn Hebrew 24 hours a day to participate in the show. I would also be really happy to represent Israel in Eurovision. But most importantly, I want them to know that I respect Israel and Israeli culture. Sometimes people accuse me of mocking religion when I upload videos about Judaism, and that's so not true."

Paytas, 33, knows what she's talking about. Even before she participated in season 20 of Big Brother UK in 2017, which she left after 11 days, she was already a sort of mini-celebrity and a significant internet personality who always provoked many reactions, both positive and negative. After appearances in several series, films, podcasts and various shows, launching a cover album, clips and singles—Paytas is a well-known name even to those who don't spend their time on YouTube. Those more familiar with the platform would argue whether she's a "troll" or a person with good intentions who is simply misunderstood, but the videos she uploads, in which she expresses her opinion on sensitive issues, often manage to provoke debates and considerable anger among viewers, and they are often discussed on gossip sites abroad as well.

Elyad! Oh My God

Paytas's connection to the Holy Land doesn't stop at watching Big Brother Israel in bits and pieces. Tal Moseri, Oren Hazan, and Tamir from Big Brother are just some of the Israelis she follows. Her latest explosive video, hold tight, is a cover she made of a song by Elyad Nechum called "Your Silence." She even invested in filming and editing an impressive clip together with her Israeli fiancé Moses Hackamon ("Moses"). Despite barely knowing a word of Hebrew, she performed the full version in the original language. Although it's hard to understand every word because of the thick accent, you can definitely say the result is satisfying.

Like all her videos, the cover of "Your Silence" generated many reactions, but one touched the star especially—from Elyad Nechum himself, who responded to her in English and wrote: "Good job with the song and with the Hebrew!" which made Paytas very happy, and she wrote back to him: "Elyad!! Oh my God, I love you so much!"

"I was very excited to see his response," she gushes, after a failed attempt to conduct the interview in Hebrew ("I speak small Hebrew"). "I was nervous because I didn't know how people in Israel would react to me and I didn't ask him for permission to do the cover. When I saw that he was enthusiastic, I was very happy because I really love him, he's a huge celebrity in my eyes. So I found clips from 'Sun' with Moses's help and saw everything I could get my hands on. He's amazing."

How did you even get to listen to Elyad's songs? "I found him on TikTok when I was searching for Hebrew duets. I learned the song to impress my fiancé, but he told me my accent wasn't good, so I listened to it again and again. Moses explained to me what the words mean so I could understand what I was saying."

Do you get to listen to Israeli music in general? "I got to listen to older songs, for example Dana International from Eurovision. I love her music but it's a bit of an old style. I also really love Neta Barzilai. I'm dying for Israeli culture, Judaism, everything related to it."

Light in Dark Times

As mentioned, Elyad wasn't the only one to respond to the cover in Hebrew. The video with its elaborate sets and effects, which accumulated about 150,000 views within days, received almost twice as many "dislikes" compared to "likes" and many comments ranging from anger to hurling insults. As mentioned, this is not the first time her videos are controversial. When asked about the reasons she thinks caused viewers to react maliciously toward her, and about the fact that it seems the trend of her videos receiving more dislikes than likes has been going on for a long time, she claims she doesn't know why, but explains that in her opinion people are stuck on who she used to be—and don't want to see her change.

"I had a lot of hate in my heart, but I changed, and people aren't ready to accept that," she says. "For me, it's fine, I always find light in dark times, and I can be a living testimony to someone who changed greatly. When I started receiving all this hate toward me, I understood that I needed to change myself and become positive, and now I meditate, choose to feel good and feel good."

"I don't really understand the conflict, but since I've been with Moses and we've been talking about Israel, people really get annoyed by it."

If Paytas truly doesn't know what caused the waves of hate toward her, or perhaps she prefers to hide the reasons, it's hard to say, as controversies have been her lot for a long time. Among other things, she announced that she identifies as transgender and feels like a gay man because she is "attracted to gay men and love glamour and shine"; that she no longer identifies as a human; asked to be referred to with plural pronouns when spoken about; used blackface. כל הדברים הללו היא עושה בתמיכת השלטון החילוני." בשנת 2000 פנה (במסגרת עמותת "אני ישראלי") למשרד הפנים וביקש להירשם תחת הלאום "ישראלי", אך בקשתו נדחתה. בסוף 2003 פתח אורנן במאבק משפטי לשינוי רישום סעיף Uzi Ornan (June 7, 1923 – November 3, 2022) was a linguist, professor of language at the Hebrew University and of natural language processing at the Technion, and a member of the Academy of the Hebrew Language. He founded the "League Against Religious Coercion," advocated for the separation of religion and state in Israel, and was identified with the Canaanite movement, whose co-founder was his brother, poet Yonatan Ratosh. 

Life and Background
Ornan was born in Jerusalem as Uziel Heilprin, son of Yechiel Heilprin, a Hebrew educator and supporter of Chaim Weizmann, and Penina, a Hebrew kindergarten teacher affiliated with Poalei Zion. His parents, two brothers, and sister immigrated to Palestine during the Third Aliyah. In his youth, he was active in the Irgun underground. In 1944, he was captured by the British and deported to detention camps in Eritrea, Sudan, and Kenya, where he remained until their closure after the establishment of the state in 1948. In the detention camps, he taught Hebrew grammar and subsequently published the textbook "Grammar of Speech and Ear—A Textbook for Hebrew Speakers." Upon his return, he began studying linguistics at the Hebrew University. In 1958, he received a master's degree for a thesis titled "Relational Words in the Poetry of H.N. Bialik." In 1965, he received a doctorate for a thesis titled "Nominal Compounds in Modern Hebrew Literature, Especially in the Prose of H.N. Bialik." The dissertation was republished in 2011 by Carmel Publishers under the title "Nominal Compounds in Modern Hebrew Literature." He was appointed lecturer and in 1972 was promoted to professor of Hebrew language. In 1979, he was elected to the Academy of the Hebrew Language, where he served until his death and headed the Committee on Punctuation Rules. In 1986, he developed the phonemic script for Hebrew, which was accepted by the International Organization for Standardization. In 1987, he was accepted as a visiting professor at the Technion's Faculty of Computer Science and began directing the Natural Language Processing Laboratory. In 1951, he was among the founders of the "League Against Religious Coercion" in Jerusalem, serving as secretary and chairman until 1967. In 1968, he brought about a court ruling that cancelled a clause in the Israel Lands Authority's lease contract that required "the lessee and all successors to refrain from all construction work and labor on the property on Sabbaths and Israeli holidays." In the 1970s, he was chairman of the secular movement founded in 1977 by Yitzhak Husson, and in the 1990s was chairman of the "I Am Israeli" organization for complete civic equality and the abolition of religious and ethnic discrimination. He died on November 3, 2022, and bequeathed his body to science.

Publications
Ornan published hundreds of articles and essays on issues of religion and state, secular and religious matters, education, and society. His books include: "Grammar of Speech and Ear," "Dictionary of Lost Words," "The Simple Sentence," "Verb Inflection in Flow Charts," "Phonetic Theory of Modern Hebrew," "The Last Word—The Mechanism of Hebrew Word Formation" (which won him the Bialik Prize), "The Fingernails of Asmodeus—Eight Chapters on Secularism," "Nominal Compounds in Modern Hebrew Literature." Among his numerous articles and essays: "Shabbat Without Chains" (1950), "Civil Marriage" (1955), "Are You Jewish" (1961).

Family
Uzi Ornan was the brother of poet Yonatan Ratosh and linguist Professor Zvi Rein. Their sister, writer Miri Dor, died young in 1945. Ornan was father to three children from his first marriage to Shoshana Malkin: Ater, Tali, and Omer. Ornan and his first wife divorced through civil divorce in the Dominican Republic. He subsequently lived with linguist Michal Afrat as a public couple, and in 1994 married her in a civil ceremony in the United States. They had a son and a daughter. His eldest daughter's daughter became religiously observant (Breslav Hasidic Judaism) and changed her name from Moran to Miriam. Since 1989, he lived in Noffit, a community in the north.

His Worldview on Religion and State
His views and actions, as expressed in numerous publications, advocated for the separation of religion and state, with concern about increasing religious coercion and the growing power of conservative bodies in Israel. Among his actions: the initiative to register "Israeli" as nationality in the identity card, support for abolishing religious criteria for Israeli citizenship, and opposition to circumcision. Ornan's views on religion and state were expressed bluntly, sometimes using militant and provocative language. He defined his position in one interview: Ornan supported separation of religion and state and strongly opposed religious coercion and those whom he saw as representing such coercion. When asked how to protest religious coercion, he answered: "There must be rebellion against this, real rebellion, with hangings from electric poles." Later in the interview, he said: "This won't work without it and I haven't changed my mind. Violence against the religious will convince them not to pursue this path"... "to hit in the full sense of the word, through economic boycott, by removing roadblocks by force on Saturdays, and by throwing them off the roads." Ornan subsequently added and detailed various practical ways to achieve his vision, such as avoiding negotiations with religious institutions, avoiding going to the rabbinate for marriages or divorces, and finding alternatives as is common abroad. Ornan argued that the religious achieved gains through force, such as preventing transportation on Saturdays and holidays on certain roads by throwing stones, and therefore proposed applying counterforce to restore traffic on those roads. Ornan's remarks about hanging from electric poles provoked protest in the Knesset and a referral to the government's legal advisor, which was rejected. In an interview conducted ten years after the first interview, he noted that it was "a figurative image" but emphasized he did not retract it, adding: "I do not believe it will be possible to get rid of the religious without using brutal force," and that "laws must be violated openly... break through the roadblocks by force. This is explicitly violence, but we must not be frightened of it... cultural war is not enough here. We must wage real war." # It's Not Just for Chefs: Stock as a Base for Soups and Stews—How Much Is It Worth Investing in Your Kitchen?

The section "On the Way to Becoming a Chef" with conclusions, tips, and recipes

These are the days of late August, hot days. In forecasts threatening a hysterical and historic heat wave about to flood all parts of the country, and we're at Danon school, in the heart of Tel Aviv's bustling port, cooking chicken stock and soups—as if it were December outside. Why exactly? I mean, why learn about this at all, rather than why didn't they postpone the lesson—that's what air conditioning is for. Chef Avihai Mizrachi explained to us that stock is actually the foundation for many dishes and techniques in the kitchen, including soups, stews, and sauces. Chicken or meat stock simmers for a relatively long time—a minimum of 3 hours for chicken stock and up to 10 hours for proper beef stock. Vegetable and fish stocks cook for shorter periods. For previous columns: Lesson 1: The day I decided to start cooking; Lesson 2: The building blocks of every kitchen; Lesson 3: Eggs, why?

For restaurants, it's clear that this investment in flavors is logical and even necessary, but is it worth making stock at home? In an era when with one click you can access countless "quick meal," "easy-peasy in the kitchen" and "pizza/challah/bouillon in ten minutes" options, how much space is there really for kitchen investment at home, and why invest so much anyway?

This is a big question that came up for me more than once before starting my cooking studies, and still comes up sometimes during the lessons too. The answer, in my view, is that investment is a subjective matter. For one person, making stock is excessive, and for another, making phyllo dough from scratch every weekend is completely reasonable.

Another point is learning and habit. That same phyllo dough would be almost impossible to make the first time, but after a few attempts it becomes a "piece of cake" recipe in itself, thus also less of a supposed "investment." This is how I learned about the precise cuts that have accompanied me for several weeks since the cutting lesson. At first it's not easy, it slows down cooking prep time and mostly frustrates—but little by little it just works out, and becomes really much more comfortable and correct.

Not what you'd think: the salad that's hardest to make at the lesson (which already better suited the heavy heat and where we learned about salads and salad dressings), Chef Chagai Larner told us, is a dish that demands a lot of investment and manpower, which is why many restaurants avoid it entirely—it's simply a green salad. Yes yes, a leafy salad. A real one, fresh and good, will be very hard to find on menus. The chef demonstrated how much time and effort it takes to select leaves, and especially to wash them properly. For many restaurants, this is an unprofitable investment. At home, it's actually a very worthwhile investment, and the salad you'll get will be refreshing, crispy and delicious—especially if you add a tangy vinaigrette and some good cheese (recipe below).

You could cut the tension with a chef's knife. The chef tastes my salads.

Back to the stock—if you do decide to make stock at home, it turns out you must not add salt at any stage (because of liquid reduction). You can freeze the stock in small containers, and this way it can serve you in the future and upgrade any dish with deep flavor. It's good to make a classic stock with basic flavors so it actually fits stews of different types. And most importantly, don't make shortcuts during cooking, and don't turn the stock into a liquid you add everything you're sad to throw away to.

We also learned that while the cut doesn't need to be precise, it is important to peel and clean the vegetables, and to keep the cut size more or less the same so they cook evenly.

We made chicken stock in class and used it for Thai soup with chicken and coconut milk—Tom Ka Gai. It's a soup that can be a whole meal. The Thai ingredients in it are very important for the taste and success of the dish, but the stock is no less important, and it's not worth skipping it.

What do you have? Invest a little bit (:

**Chicken Stock**

Ingredients for 5.5 liters of stock:
• 2 kg chicken bones/wings
• 2 onions
• 2 stalks of celery
• 2 carrots
• 1 leek
• 10 garlic cloves
• 1 large bouquet garni: parsley, thyme, bay leaves
• 1 clove
• 10 white peppercorns
• 6 liters of water

Preparation:
1. Put the chicken in water and bring to a boil. Skim the foam that rises with a slotted spoon.
2. Cut the vegetables: onion into rings, carrot and celery roughly chopped. Pierce the clove into one of the onion pieces so it doesn't "get lost" in the pot.
3. Prepare the bouquet garni (herb bundle): arrange bay leaves, parsley stems and thyme inside a leek leaf.
4. When the chicken has produced enough foam, add the vegetables, garlic cloves and herb bundle.
5. Simmer for 3 hours and strain the contents.

**Coconut, Galangal and Chicken Soup (Tom Ka Gai)**

Ingredients for 3 servings:
• 250 grams chicken stock
• 70 grams boneless chicken breast cut into strips
• 200 grams coconut milk
• 2 kaffir lime leaves
• 1 shallot, finely minced
• 1 stalk lemongrass, finely minced
• 1 slice galangal (or ginger if unavailable)
• Half a red chili, finely minced
• 6 cilantro stems, chopped + leaves for serving
• 2 tablespoons fish sauce
• 1 tablespoon palm sugar
• 1 lime/lemon juice
• 80 grams oyster mushrooms torn/roughly chopped
• 5 cherry tomatoes, halved

Preparation:
1. Bring the chicken stock to a boil in a pot with the shallot, galangal, lemongrass, cilantro and chili.
2. After boiling, add the sugar, coconut milk and fish sauce.
3. Add the mushrooms and tomatoes and bring back to a boil.
4. Add lime juice and taste to adjust seasoning.
5. Just before serving, add the chicken strips and simmer for about two minutes until cooked through.
6. Serve with cilantro leaves on top with a green salad with herb vinaigrette.

• 600 grams mixed greens (recommended: romaine, iceberg, arugula, endive, mâche)
• 50 grams hard cheese with strong flavor (Parmesan, blue cheese)
• 2 pears, thinly sliced
• 4 tablespoons toasted pecan nuts

• 2 tablespoons honey
• 1 teaspoon thyme leaves
• 1 teaspoon tarragon leaves (not essential)
• 2 tablespoons Dijon mustard
• 8 tablespoons olive oil
• 8 tablespoons neutral oil

Come with Me to the Festival

On Thursday the Haifa Film Festival will open • A house correspondent recommends a few films to be screened there

The 30th edition of the Haifa Film Festival, opening this coming Thursday with a screening of "The Judge," starring Robert Downey Jr. and Robert Duvall, offers this year a long and almost exaggerated array of fascinating and recommended films.

Want more updates? Join Israel Today on Facebook

Besides an intriguing Israeli competition featuring, among others, "A Good Death" by Sharon Maymon and Tal Granit, "Jonah" by Nir Bergman, "You to Me at Night" by Assaf Korman, and "Manpower" by Noam Kaplan, and besides a visit by the excellent Russian director Andrei Zvyagintsev ("The Return," "The Banishment"), who will present his acclaimed new film "Leviathan," the festival will also screen some of the most talked-about works of the past year, such as "Winter Sleep" by Nuri Bilge Ceylan ("Once Upon a Time in Anatolia"), which won the Palme d'Or at the recent Cannes Festival, and the American "Whiplash," which won the grand prize at the Sundance Festival.

To make it easier for you to navigate the rich program, here are a few more films, somewhat less known, that are definitely worth being aware of.

• "20,000 Days on Earth": Singer-poet-writer-screenwriter Nick Cave has disappeared somewhat in recent years, but this thrilling, stylish and inspiring musical biography, which stands somewhere between an artistic documentary and a self-portrait, is sure to delight and move anyone who has been captivated by his unique charm over the years. Directors Ian Forsyth and Jane Pollard take Cave on a journey to the past, send him to sift through archive photos, introduce him to prominent figures he collaborated with (such as Björk Guðmundsdóttir and Kylie Minogue) and accompany him as he works on his new album. Cave, who turned 57 this year, opens up to the camera, reveals fascinating details about his creative process, philosophizes as if there were no tomorrow, and of course, also sings. A huge film about a huge artist.

• "Ida": After several decades of working in England, Polish director Paweł Pawlikowski returns to his homeland to present a stunning black-and-white drama set in the early 1960s. At the center of the plot stands a young and innocent nun who sets out with her Jewish (and communist) aunt on a roots journey in search of her family who were murdered during the Nazi occupation. Through stunning monochromatic cinematography and superb performances by the two women, Pawlikowski creates a tight and precise film containing enormous amounts of sorrow and guilt. "Ida" arrives in Haifa after garnering praise at countless festivals and after being earmarked as a leading candidate for winning the Best Foreign Film Oscar at the upcoming ceremony. In its case, the hype is completely justified.

• "Like Cattle": British director David Mackenzie ("Spread," "Perfect Sense") may not be particularly consistent, but his new film is undoubtedly one of his best. It's a visceral, violent and unexpected prison drama that follows Eric (Jake O'Connell), an angry young prisoner who is placed in a detention facility meant for adult inmates. The fact that his father (Ben Mendelsohn), whom he hasn't seen since he was five, is also imprisoned there, is supposed to help him survive, but in reality only makes things more complicated and dangerous. O'Connell (expected to become a star following his appearance here) and Mendelsohn ("Killing Them Softly") simply set the screen on fire, and Mackenzie manages to make the charged relationship that develops between them complex, extraordinary and unforgettable.

• "Clouds of Sils Maria": French director Olivier Assayas ("Irma Vep," "Summer Hours," "Carlos") is also not known for consistency, but as in Mackenzie's case, he too is at peak form in his new film. Juliette Binoche plays an aging film star, Kristen Stewart plays her personal assistant, and Assayas uses both of them to delicately and mockingly probe the creative process, performance, aging and female jealousy. Binoche delivers one of her best performances in recent years. The excellent Stewart proves there is life after "Twilight," and Chloë Grace Moretz ("Kick-Ass"), who appears in a guest role, also manages to leave her mark. The result is elegant, enigmatic and thought-provoking, and if you wish, you can see it as the feminine version of "Molière on a Bicycle."

• "Killer Joe": Michael C. Hall ("Dexter"), Sam Shepard and Don Johnson star in a dark and trashy Texas thriller from horror director Jim Mickle (responsible for the American remake of the Mexican cannibal film "We Are What We Are"). A law-abiding family man kills a burglar who broke into his home and finds himself swept into a violent and chilling maelstrom involving corrupt cops, gangsters and snuff films. On paper you've already seen this film before, but Mickle and his regular screenwriter Nick Damici navigate the work in surprising directions. The three leads gleefully commit themselves to the apparently inferior material, and genre fans are sure to leave the theater with a sickly smile.

• "Corn Island": The big winner at the Karlovy Vary Festival is a film festival par excellence. It takes place entirely on a small island in the Mtkvari River that separates Georgia from Abkhazia, has almost no dialogue, and most of its minutes are devoted to methodically following an old man and his granddaughter engaged in agricultural work. Yet if you fancy diving into a fascinating and very special cinematic experience, and you are blessed with a bit more patience than average, "Corn Island" by Giorgi Ovsiannikov, which tells a simple parable about man, nature and eternal political conflicts, is undoubtedly the film for you.

• "Truffaut Forever": Alongside some of the greatest works of legendary French director François Truffaut ("Two English Girls," "Jules and Jim" and "The 400 Blows"), to be screened at the festival marking 30 years since his death, this new documentary, directed by Alexandre Moua, will also be screened. You won't find earth-shattering revelations here, but through old interviews with the great director, perusal of his personal letters and conversations with his friends and colleagues, Moua's delicate, modest and not very long work sketches a moving human portrait of a great filmmaker and awakens a strong desire to watch again the splendid body of his work.

# Survivor: Everyone Against Everyone

The public auction arrived just in time to show us that from now on it's every survivor for themselves • Coming soon: our bets on the finale • Episodes 44-45 on Matcha

Friends, we're excited to announce - the finale is around the corner. Of course, by "around the corner" we mean you still need to travel dozens more hours through an endless stream of mind-numbing events, take a turn at the "Villa of the Eliminated," stop at "Big Disputes Square," and get stuck at dozens of special traffic lights on the way to the finale. In short, despite there already being an estimated date, there's still a long way to go, and during which, judging by the promo, the survivors will manage to switch alliances like socks. We're in any case starting to bet on who makes it to the finale, but we'll save that for a separate column, if you don't mind.

## A New Era

In Tuesday's episode, the survivors are also starting to smell the finale - Assi is displaying an outward demeanor of calm, but internally he's already divvying up the jury votes. It's not good for him to reach the finale with his allies, since they're actually the ones who could vote for him as jurors, while continuing his competition with them will be a struggle for jury votes already eliminated. They ate from the same trough and that's it.

Assi made a clever and rather surprising move and turned to form an alliance with Eden. The fact that he initiated it perhaps makes him more "dirty," but it's a strategically brilliant move and Eden the tycoon understands this too and was happy to cooperate. This is double risk, because beyond the fact that they need to eliminate their friends delicately so the jurors don't turn against them, they're now dependent on each other's mercy. Assi didn't hesitate to betray his friends in the past, and Eden might still surprise.

In the negotiation hut, Alina befriends herself with her feelings, and gives us another gaping mouth, discovering that she needs to eat a huge bowl of peanut butter to beat Ragev. On the agenda - a conversation with Rafael Chavibi (father of), who understands that Alina's staying will help Eden more and decides to encourage her specifically. Ragev also doesn't seem eager to win the challenge, and Alina scores a first and significant victory.

## Survivor: Island Wretches

## Survivor: What If?

But does the alliance situation get shaken up again like a sponge? Because here Jordan turns to Assi and offers him... wait, what did she offer him? It was something like "I won't leave my alliance and you won't leave yours, but I enjoy watching you play and maybe we'll do something." We didn't understand - do you want to exercise together? Sign up for a macramé class? Join "Bozglos"? Bottom line, Jordan wanted to go and feel free, and Assi gently waved her off, just like a Tinder chat where it's clear it's going nowhere and the other side says "we'll talk tomorrow," really meaning "let's pretend this never happened."

Let's jump ahead to the next duel challenge, which Alina entered skipping. Pier - despite barely seeing her five minutes - we missed her. After Ragev gets irritated for a moment over the word "twisted" ("Why twisted? What did I twist?"), Alina decides to continue their riveting romance and takes him on another challenge. Against the backdrop of a recently published interview with past survivor Omer Rozen, who spoke about how the production wanted competitors' praise, received immunity challenges that seem tailored to their measurements, it's hard not to wonder if this challenge too is at least comfortable for Alina, the dancer with strong stability. Unsurprisingly, she wins and takes Ragev's vote, causing a flip in votes and now Eden and Jordan's alliance is leading.

## Eating the Cake and Keeping It Whole

Saturday's episode opens with Ella's sad confession about struggling to form meaningful connections with girls throughout her life, and we promise if she didn't get a nasty sentence toward someone in the coming episodes, we might start liking her. But never mind - the main course in this episode is the public auction challenge, which is always fun to watch.

A moment before - the social ranking that's not really relevant to anyone except the one ranked last. In this case it's as expected Beni, who was denied participation. Pier, there's nothing worse than that.

We won't mention all the packages, but here are some moments we especially loved:

**The nicest moment:** The "player card" that Eden Chavibi bought, allowing him to either bring Beni into the game or get extra money for himself. Eden of course chooses the friendly/smart strategic move to include Beni in the game. While Israel was quick to bite at the fact that it's all strategy in the food chain, and that Eden doesn't really love Beni, hey - immediately after that karma gave Eden a slap. There's justice in the world.

**The funniest moment:** In this case it's every single one of Ragev's purchases, where Gia kept giving him the chance to swap the package he chose for another, and he kept staying with his choices, until the moment when the weak one lifted and he discovered "essential" items like Botox injections and dental floss. And we thought Beni was the comic character of the season.

**The most-actually-funniest moment:** But with all due respect to Ragev's blunders, Ella fell big into Gia's trap when he announced a package that makes him do rotational movements. And this after she won the useful "makeup-hair" package, right? She sent 650 pesos toward Gia and squealed toward him in joy, but when the weak one was lifted it turned out to be a picture of hummus and not the real thing. "How could you do this to me?" she blurted out in offense, and after the sense of discomfort passed over us, we had to be lifted off the floor from laughing.

**The most delicious moment:** Jordan waited and waited and at some point it became annoying - where's your sportsmanship? But like in competitions against a tough female judoka from a foreign country, Jordan knew exactly what she was doing. She waited for the right moment, and then when the package that caught her attention arrived, there weren't many competitors left and Jordan managed to buy two enormous portions - pitas and a platter of salads, and a roll with sausage plus beer. The beer is to hide your eyes from the other survivors. Still, how delicious - it's not that pleasant.

**The most horrifying moment:** In the final minutes of the episode, when it was already clear the challenge was about to end, Beni offered to buy the cake for everyone, and the merciful and gracious Gia agreed to provide a happy ending to today's episode, and called Ella to take the cake and serve everyone. Mmm, while she's walking toward the survivors with the cake she dipped a finger in the cake to taste, began to slip and for one horrible moment the cake began to slide and almost fell. Lucky that Ella managed to straighten herself in time. In the end she still mumbled "I'm okay." Bottom line, there are courses that could go down the drain.

Finally, let's comment on the change of name to the promo that in direct continuation of the previous episode's events presents the renewed tribe division plan. So, according to the promo (and only according to it, yes?), Assi tries to pull Beni back to them while Ragev might join Jordan altogether. We're actually not at all sure any of these moves actually happened, but one thing's for sure - the next eliminations will get as dramatic as we get closer to the finale. After all, a million shekels.

"The best thing for Assi Bozglo is for his alliance to go home, Assi Bozglo today is looking for the best way to reach the finale"

"He saw my heart in the game and it shows how much heart here can win" (Alina about Rafael - correct, if she means the heart of a bat)

"You're the only parent doing it opposite from everyone else" (Ragev educating Rafael)

"I thought they gave him crocodile eggs to eat" (Israel doesn't understand why Ragev couldn't eat two tons of peanut butter)

"Did you finally manage to light a fire?" (Gia to Alina. Let's see you, Mister Host)

"Less than 24 hours she's there telling about a deep emotional process she's going through in the hut" (Assi, also knows how to talk about others, not just himself)

"I'm your friend" (Israel to Ella. It took time, but finally Jonah Welch made it to "Survivor")

Beni: "If he's laughing without me even throwing a single punch, that's it guys, I'm in the right profession"

Gia: "Actually from your punches I'm not laughing" (Let's see you, Mister Host #2)

"Gia, can you register me until the land?" (Ragev, clarifying if the public auction is also in the surrounding area)

"I'm taking Beni an egg in a second" (Ella, albeit irritating, but still would have been better phrased differently)

"If they ask you what sign you are, answer Pisces" (Israel, summing up Ragev's string of successes in the challenge)

"תהליך הסרת השיער באמצעות קרן אור מבוסס על עיקרון בשם 'תרמוליזה' - הפיכת אנרגיית אור לאנרגיית חום, אשר נבלעת במלנין של השערה ומוליכה אותו לזקיק", הסביר ערן שלינגבאום, סמנכ"ל מוצרים ופיתוח עסקי בחברת אמריקן לייזר, "כמטאפורה, קרן האור מועברת באמצעות השערה, המשמשת אנטנה, לזקיק השערה ומנתקת ביניהם. בדרך זו הזקיק מפסיק להצמיח שערות חדשות. חשוב לציין שהמונח 'הסרת שיער לצמיתות' אינו נכון ולא מדויק. לא ניתן להסיר שיער לצמיתות, היות שבגוף יש מאות אלפי זקיקי שיער ורק אלפי זקיקים פעילים. בטיפול עצמו אנו מטפלים בזקיקים הקיימים, אך ייתכן מצב שבו זקיקים רדומים יתעוררו ויצמיחו שיער בשל שינויים הורמונליים, גיל וטיפול לא נכון". תוצאות שונות לכל אדם אחת השיטות הפופולריות ביותר בתחום היא IPL - טכנולוגיה המפזרת את קרן האור בצורת פעמון, מכסה שטח גדול ומתאימה לבעלי גוון עור בהיר או שחום, ולבעלי שיער דק או עבה. עם זאת, היא אינה חודרת לשכבות התת־עוריות של העור ולא מתמקדת בזקיק שערה בודד. היא מתאימה לטיפולים בכלל אזורי הגוף. שיטה פופולרית נוספת היא DPC - קרן אור מתקדמת יותר עם יכולות ועוצמות גבוהות יותר מ־IPL, הנותנת מענה של תצורת פולס אינדיבידואלית ללקוח הספציפי. שיטה זו מגיעה לשכבות עמוקות יותר של העור מ־IPL ומתאימה למרבית גוני העור וסוגי השיער השונים. שני סוגי המכשירים מכילים מערכת קירור מובנית בתוך המכשיר, המפחיתה באופן משמעותי תחושת כאב ואי־נעימות. חשוב להבין כי לא כל מכשיר הפועל בשיטת IPL ייתן אותה תוצאה עבור הלקוח, טיב התוצאות משתנה מאדם לאדם. שתי הטכנולוגיות הנפוצות והמקובלות להסרת שיער מבוססות על קרן אור, וההבדל ביניהן בא לידי ביטוי בשני פרמטרים מרכזיים. הראשון הוא צורת הקרן: קרן הלייזר יורדת באורך גל יחיד (ללא פיזור) או מפזרת את קרן האור בצורת פעמון המכסה שטח גדול עם אורכי גל שונים. הפרמטר השני הוא עומק חדירת הקרן - עומק ההגעה של הקרן לתוך שכבת העור. החדירה נמדדת בננומטרים ובהתאמה לכל מכשיר ומטופל, המבצעים מגדירים מהו עומק החדירה שלהם. שני סוגי ביצוע הסרת השיער הם הפופולריים ביותר. הראשון שבהם הוא Alexandrit - המתאים לבעלי עור בהיר (גוון עור 1 עד 3). קרן האור מגיעה לעומק של 755 ננומטר, והמכשיר עובד עם מערכת קירור צמודה להעור. השני הוא DIODE - המתאים לגווני עור 5-1 ועובד בעומק חדירה של 810 ננומטר. זוהי הטכנולוגיה שעימה החל התחום לפעול בישראל ובעולם בסוף שנות ה־90, וברוב המקרים כולל מערכת קירור מובנית בידית. גאווה ישראלית ערן שלינגבאום מוסיף בגאווה כי "הנקודה הישראלית המעניינת בנושא היא שהיצרנים הישראלים נחשבים למתקדמים ולמובילים בתחום ברחבי העולם". יש לא מעט חברות ישראליות שמייצרות וממציאות מכשירים כאלה ומוכרות בכל העולם. ואם בגאווה עסקינן, שיטה חדשה שהיא כל כולה פיתוח כחול־לבן מקצרת משמעותית את זמן הטיפול, בשל העובדה הפשוטה שאין בה צורך במריחת ג'ל. חברת מד־אופ, המתמחה זה 32 בייצור מכשירים להסרת שיער, מציעה בדרך זו טיפול לכל הגוף ב־20 דקות בלבד. יתרון נוסף שיש במכשיר שכזה הוא היכולת לעשות טיפול אפילו באמצע יום עבודה ולא לחוש אי־נוחות בגלל הג'ל. את הסטורי שלנו כבר בדקתם היום? הצטרפו כאן לאינסטגרם של ישראל היום אחד מבעלי מד־אופ, שלמה שרון, הסביר מדוע היה חשוב לפתח את מכשיר זה. "שיטת ה־SHR עובדת על ידי הבזקי אור שמקרינים על הרקמה ועל המלנין של השערה. העובדים בשיטה זו משתמשים בידית שתפקידה לקרר את הרקמה בזמן שעובדים עליה. לדעתי, מערכת הקירור, שהכרחית בשיטה זו, גורעת מאיכות הטיפול בה. בתחום ההסרה אנחנו שואפים תמיד להגיע לזקיק השערה, ב־70 מעלות, ואם אני מקרר רקמה בזמן שהחום הוא של 37 מעלות - התוצאה תהיה הרבה פחות טובה". חברה ישראלית נוספת, שהסירה שערות רבות מהרבה אנשים בשנות קיומה, היא "לומינס". לדעת שירי סלומון, גלובל דירקטור בתחום הסרת שיער בחברה, הצרכנים הישראלים "היו מהראשונים לאמץ את הטרנד העולמי של הסרת שיער בלייזר, וכתוצאה מכך תחום זה מאוד רווח בישראל. אנחנו רואים את גיל צרכני הסרת השיער הולך ויורד. למעשה, אנו רואים היום ילדות בנות 12 ומעלה שמגיעות עם האימהות שלהן לטיפולים משותפים של הסרת שיער בלייזר. הן מחפשות טיפול מהיר, שאינו כואב ויעיל כדוגמת מכשיר הלייטשיר (LightSheer) של לומניס, המאפשר טיפול בשטח גדול בכמה דקות בלבד וללא כאב". היעדר פיקוח יש מגוון עצום של קוסמטיקאיות ומכונים המציעים את השירות, שזה אחד היתרונות והחסרונות הבולטים בשוק. אין שום פיקוח על מכשירי הסרת השיער, ובשנים האחרונות חלה עלייה משמעותית בקניית מכשירים כאלה באינטרנט, מה שהוריד עוד יותר את הפיקוח, ומנגד העלה את הסיכון. עצם העובדה שבחלק גדול מהמקרים הטיפולים מבוצעים על ידי קוסמטיקאיות ולא על ידי רופאים היא בעייתית, בגלל הנזקים שיכולים להיגרם. אין זה אומר שקוסמטיקאית לא יכולה לבצע טיפול שכזה, אך מומלץ לצרכן לבדוק את רמת המקצועיות שלה, וחשוב לא פחות של איזו חברה מכשיר ההסרה ומניין הוא נקנה. זו הסיבה שמכונים מסוימים מקפידים שהטיפולים הללו ייעשו אך ורק על ידי רופאים. שלמה שרון וחברת מד־אופ מוכרים את המכשירים למכונים גדולים ולקוסמטיקאיות פרטיות מכיוון שהוא מודע היטב לסיכונים, וחברתו מקפידה מאוד שכל מי שרוכשת ממנה מכשיר תעבור הכשרה מקיפה. מד־אופ עצמה מבטחת אותן, מטפלת במכשירים ומחייבת אותן ברענון של הדרכות. בד בבד, עליהן לעבור מבחן הסמכה לפני שהן מתחילות לטפל. # Summer Hair-Free: All About Hair Removal

Summer exposes us, and many—not just women—seek smooth skin. The market offers a variety of body hair removal solutions—we examined the options.

Many reasons exist to love summer, but several do the opposite. Hair removal is one of them, and since it's solvable, we set out to examine the market and report on current options. In recent years, the permanent hair removal industry has developed at an accelerated pace, with specialized clinics opening at a dizzying rate. The dominant market trend recently includes, alongside clinic operations, private aestheticians who have brought appropriate devices into their clinics, competing with clinics. Recently joining clinics and aestheticians: home devices. The problem peaks in summer, but you typically need to start addressing it in winter. This is because most permanent hair removal techniques irritate the skin, and sun exposure during treatment causes pigmentation—skin spots. Therefore, it's highly recommended that those undergoing laser hair removal avoid tanning for several days after treatment and use the highest possible sun protection factor, at least SPF 30. If previously we had to stay home to achieve the desired result—smooth, hair-free skin—today it's simply much easier. The market is full of promotions, from vouchers offering discounted treatment packages to clinics offering attractive deals due to device proliferation and accessibility. To organize this flood of information and types, we'll take you hair by hair through the field. Currently, several ways to remove hair permanently exist on the market. However—and this is a big however before we continue—there's no such thing as permanent hair removal. Not all hair disappears forever; most will disappear for a long period but it's possible that in a few years you'll need to repeat treatment. During treatment, some hair is dormant, in which a follicle exists but doesn't produce hair; such hair can "awaken" and start growing regardless of treatment for various reasons, including hormonal changes, stress, childbirth, age, medication use, and health changes. Additionally, since this technology is largely based on color differences between hair and skin, treatment won't be equally effective for everyone. Certain body areas present special challenges, including the face, shoulders, and neck, due to hair structure in these areas and hormonal effects. One of the most important parameters for the success of such treatments is skin tone, measured by an index called "Fitzpatrick scale," which ranks tones 1-6, with 1 being the lightest and 6 the darkest.

## Choose Medical Experience

Dr. Anna Kushnier, a diagnostic physician in hair removal and medical devices and national domain manager for "Clalit Aesthetics," explained that "in hair removal, laser treatments exist in many unofficial locations, such as beauty salons, spas, and casual clinics, but it's very important to choose clinics with medical experience. Laser hair removal should be performed by experienced medical staff trained for this. When laser treatment is done under medical supervision, and only a specialist doctor approves treatment for a patient, the likelihood of complications is zero." Nevertheless, side effects like discomfort, swelling, and redness lasting several days can occur, and in some cases, temporary dark or light spots may appear, especially in tanned patients or those with dark skin. Kushnier added that "to reduce the risk of side effects, you must follow your treating doctor's post-treatment instructions. Other possible complications, though extremely rare, are paradoxically accelerated hair growth, forcing the doctor to change treatment technology or stop it, first and second-degree burns resulting from sun exposure, and accelerated or slowed pigmentation or appearance of pigmentation in the treated area. This problem usually disappears over time, and only rarely does it become permanent."

## How It Works

"Hair removal via light beam is based on a principle called 'thermolysis'—converting light energy into heat energy, which is absorbed by hair melanin and conducts it to the follicle," explained Eran Shlingbaum, VP Products and Business Development at American Laser. "As a metaphor, the light beam is transmitted through the hair, serving as an antenna, to the hair follicle and disconnects between them. This way, the follicle stops producing new hair. It's important to note that the term 'permanent hair removal' is incorrect and inaccurate. Hair cannot be removed permanently, as the body has hundreds of thousands of hair follicles with only thousands active. In treatment itself, we address existing follicles, but dormant follicles may awaken and produce hair due to hormonal changes, age, and incorrect treatment."

## Different Results for Each Person

One of the most popular methods is IPL—technology that disperses the light beam fan-shaped, covers large areas, and suits those with light or tanned skin and thin or thick hair. However, it doesn't penetrate subcutaneous skin layers and doesn't target individual hair follicles. It's suitable for treating all body areas. Another popular method is DPC—an advanced light beam with higher capabilities and power than IPL, providing individualized pulse configuration for specific clients. This method reaches deeper skin layers than IPL and suits most skin tones and hair types. Both device types contain built-in cooling systems reducing pain and discomfort significantly. It's important to understand that not every device operating on IPL will give the same result; quality varies person to person.

Two common, accepted hair removal technologies are based on light beams, with differences in two central parameters. The first is beam shape: laser beam travels in single wavelength (no dispersion) or disperses light fan-shaped covering large areas with different wavelengths. The second parameter is beam penetration depth—how deep the beam reaches into skin layers. Penetration is measured in nanometers and adapted to each device and patient, with practitioners defining their penetration depth. Two types of hair removal procedures are most popular.

The first is Alexandrit—suitable for those with light skin (skin tone 1-3). The light beam reaches 755 nanometers depth, and the device works with a cooling system attached to skin. The second is DIODE—suitable for skin tones 1-5, operating at 810 nanometer penetration depth. This is the technology with which the field began operating in Israel and worldwide in the late 90s, and in most cases includes built-in cooling in the handpiece.

Med-Op, specializing for 32 years in hair removal device manufacturing, offers this way full-body treatment in just 20 minutes. An additional advantage of such a device is the ability to receive treatment even mid-workday without gel discomfort.

Another Israeli company, having removed hair from many people during its existence, is "Lumenis." According to Shiri Solomon, global director of hair removal at the company, Israeli consumers "were among the first adopting the global trend of laser hair removal, and consequently this field is very profitable in Israel. # Falafel or Baguette? Michele Kishka's New Graphic Novel

In a pita or a baguette? Michele Kishka's new graphic novel attempts to tell the story of Israeli "we," while stepping through foundational events • His narrator, an immigrant who fell in love with Israel and longs for what it was, complicates the task from the moment we look at the cover of "Falafel with Hot Sauce," Michele Kishka's new graphic-autobiographical novel, a difference is evident between his new creation and his previous graphic book, "The Second Generation—Things I Didn't Tell Dad" (Modan/Chargol, 2013). If black and white colors adorned the cover of the previous Holocaust novel, which dealt with Kishka's life as the son of a Holocaust survivor, and his figure stood alone on the cover with Auschwitz concentration camp in the background—in "Falafel with Hot Sauce" color dominates. Gray skies are replaced by a bright sky and a crowded celebration of Israeli masses packed on the cover between "Peace Now" signs and "Shabbat" ones. The "I" has been replaced with "we." And what is more the story of the "we" than the book's title, which flutters on the cover? For Kishka, an illustrator, comic and caricature artist, the "general," in this case the story of becoming Israeli and documenting Israeli experience, is always political, serving as a mirror to document a larger social picture steeped in warm humor. What Kishka briefly noted in a paragraph in "The Second Generation," he expands into a full novel: "I decided to leave everything, I came up to the land, was accepted to Bezalel, finished a degree in graphic design, during my studies I met Olivia, we got married and had David."

The book cover opens in the summer of 1969, on his character's first visit to his aunt Paula, sowing the seeds of his love affair in Tel Aviv: "Thirty-five degrees in the shade, the shirt sticks to my body, I feel wonderful." In his European innocence, a foreign child in a candy shop, falafel balls seem to him like meatballs, to which the vendor's generous spoonfuls of spicy liquid are added, which Kishka mistakenly thinks is tomato sauce. That very humorous mistake, illustrated in charming pen, will symbolize Kishka's initial groping and later confident path through Israeli ways. He insists on discovering them despite difficulties of mentality, language, and culture. Frame after frame, square after square, he illustrates Israeli symbols: the choice not to join the Christian Scouting movement like most of his friends in Liaise but to join the Young Guard movement; volunteering on a kibbutz; a Bar Mitzvah celebration a month after the victory of the Six-Day War; a sense of pioneering and mission on journeys throughout the length and breadth of the land; sunrise over Mount Nebo; the first kiss on the farm. The narrator defines this fascination with Israel and the meticulous desire to document his experiences as an irrational, wonderful but not religious love affair. "Holiness is a concept completely foreign to me. I was drawn to physical Israel, not the celestial one," he testifies. That same wonderfulness, his being a "hybrid type, a mixture of two cultures," the abnormality that comprises Israel, "which is in a state of constant warfare but aspires to peace with its neighbors," he expresses through gestures toward surrealist works like "The Treachery of Images" and "The Son of Man" by his countryman, Belgian Magritte, and thus saves that patriotism from banality. The abandonment of socialist values, which cultivate productivity and do not align with Kishka's longing for spiritual life and comic creation ("reactionary and bourgeois," thus members of the movement label the medium in a sentence they deliver to the young artist, who in one of the amusing frames returns to his room to look up the word's meaning in a dictionary) and leaving Kibbutz Ravdim, sharpen one of the central axes around which the novel revolves: pragmatism and productivity. These are expressed in warfare, manual labor, or Kishka's temporary choice of profession in productive and "meaningful" fields, such as architecture. If you will, life versus art. Without the physical ability to fight, Kishka chooses to channel his anger on the stadium walls of Standard Liaise team, on which he writes "Israel will win." Thus, in '74, when he is nineteen, he formally immigrates to the Land of Israel and is drafted for shortened military service, and convinces his commander that it will be more useful to him "with a paintbrush in hand than with an M-16."

When his wife Olivia goes out to "Peace Now" demonstrations, he notes: "Olivia demonstrated for peace and I painted for peace."

Is caricature a central player in culture and its maintenance? Kishka with caricaturist Plantu during his visit to Israel. Photo: Koko

The question of whether political caricature has the power to create and dictate an agenda, and whether it is a central player in the maintenance and development of culture, is woven as a second thread through the novel. If you ask Kishka, a member of "Cartoonists for Peace," founded by his French cartoonist friend Plantu, and in which they fight for freedom of creative expression, the answer echoes yes. The last part, and in my view the most successful in the book, Kishka dedicates at relative length to his work as a political cartoonist and the creative process. He meets cartoonists from around the world, persecuted for their work and the criticism they leveled against their home governments. He illustrates his colleagues and notes the reason for their persecution. Through their stories, no less, the meager Israeli caricature culture is highlighted, especially when Kishka notes his colleagues murdered in the attack on the offices of the satirical newspaper "Charlie Hebdo." Not for nothing does the book end at this point, as if wanting to emphasize the force of the shock, the watershed line that, despite the tragedy inherent in it, does not relax Kishka's hand. Like "The Second Generation," this book also expresses Kishka's talent for building a multi-layered story from places and items of reality; the reader moves with him from one war to another, from the murder of Emil Grunzweig to the assassination of Rabin, one Intifada chasing another, while the round, warm line, almost entirely devoid of black contour, gives the reading experiences cinematic qualities. Aesthetically, the European tradition from which the illustrator draws is evident, maintaining realistic fullness—from illustrating the newspapers of that period, clothing, the red-windowed frame of "Bezalel." It seems the protagonist in this book is aware of his privileged status and does not try to hide it, perhaps even proud of it. The veteran lecturer, who raised generations of illustrators, mourns that he has become an archaeological fossil, a secular and leftist Jew, an "extinct species" in his phrasing. He illustrates himself compressed in formaldehyde like a laboratory animal. It seems that at times the quality of the illustrations surpasses the strength of the words, and they appear as decoration to the visuals or fail in cliché. This is evident, for example, when Olivia is wounded at the demonstration in which Grunzweig is murdered, and her "scar healed over time but the tear in Israeli society remains gaping," or when the protagonist declares: "God is quite a DJ who wants everyone on the dance floor." The choice to create an illustrated account that purports to cover more than 30 years, rather than focus on an event or focused memory, is sometimes against the book's grain. Kishka said in an interview that he deliberately aimed at readers across the sea as well, and it shows. This is because Kishka's protagonist often seems like a satisfied bourgeois yearning for a period that will never return. Also the choice not to divide the book into chapters (unlike "The Second Generation") creates a sense of excess and quick passage between events. And yet, it is an original, important, and groundbreaking work. One might wonder why graphic-historical novels are absent from Israeli bookshelves, and why there is an almost immediate tendency for Israeli comic creators to only deal with "here and now." In addition to Kishka's audacity, the book provides a loving, compassionate, funny, and despairing mirror of Israelis.

Falafel with Hot Sauce / Michele Kishka; Modan, 96 pages

Come with Me to the Festival

On Thursday the Haifa Film Festival will open • A house correspondent recommends a few films to be screened there

The 30th edition of the Haifa Film Festival, opening this coming Thursday with a screening of "The Judge," starring Robert Downey Jr. and Robert Duvall, offers this year a long and almost exaggerated array of fascinating and recommended films.

Want more updates? Join Israel Today on Facebook

Besides an intriguing Israeli competition featuring, among others, "A Good Death" by Sharon Maymon and Tal Granit, "Jonah" by Nir Bergman, "You to Me at Night" by Assaf Korman, and "Manpower" by Noam Kaplan, and besides a visit by the excellent Russian director Andrei Zvyagintsev ("The Return," "The Banishment"), who will present his acclaimed new film "Leviathan," the festival will also screen some of the most talked-about works of the past year, such as "Winter Sleep" by Nuri Bilge Ceylan ("Once Upon a Time in Anatolia"), which won the Palme d'Or at the recent Cannes Festival, and the American "Whiplash," which won the grand prize at the Sundance Festival.

To make it easier for you to navigate the rich program, here are a few more films, somewhat less known, that are definitely worth being aware of.

• "20,000 Days on Earth": Singer-poet-writer-screenwriter Nick Cave has disappeared somewhat in recent years, but this thrilling, stylish and inspiring musical biography, which stands somewhere between an artistic documentary and a self-portrait, is sure to delight and move anyone who has been captivated by his unique charm over the years. Directors Ian Forsyth and Jane Pollard take Cave on a journey to the past, send him to sift through archive photos, introduce him to prominent figures he collaborated with (such as Björk Guðmundsdóttir and Kylie Minogue) and accompany him as he works on his new album. Cave, who turned 57 this year, opens up to the camera, reveals fascinating details about his creative process, philosophizes as if there were no tomorrow, and of course, also sings. A huge film about a huge artist.

• "Ida": After several decades of working in England, Polish director Paweł Pawlikowski returns to his homeland to present a stunning black-and-white drama set in the early 1960s. At the center of the plot stands a young and innocent nun who sets out with her Jewish (and communist) aunt on a roots journey in search of her family who were murdered during the Nazi occupation. Through stunning monochromatic cinematography and superb performances by the two women, Pawlikowski creates a tight and precise film containing enormous amounts of sorrow and guilt. "Ida" arrives in Haifa after garnering praise at countless festivals and after being earmarked as a leading candidate for winning the Best Foreign Film Oscar at the upcoming ceremony. In its case, the hype is completely justified.

• "Like Cattle": British director David Mackenzie ("Spread," "Perfect Sense") may not be particularly consistent, but his new film is undoubtedly one of his best. It's a visceral, violent and unexpected prison drama that follows Eric (Jake O'Connell), an angry young prisoner who is placed in a detention facility meant for adult inmates. The fact that his father (Ben Mendelsohn), whom he hasn't seen since he was five, is also imprisoned there, is supposed to help him survive, but in reality only makes things more complicated and dangerous. O'Connell (expected to become a star following his appearance here) and Mendelsohn ("Killing Them Softly") simply set the screen on fire, and Mackenzie manages to make the charged relationship that develops between them complex, extraordinary and unforgettable.

• "Clouds of Sils Maria": French director Olivier Assayas ("Irma Vep," "Summer Hours," "Carlos") is also not known for consistency, but as in Mackenzie's case, he too is at peak form in his new film. Juliette Binoche plays an aging film star, Kristen Stewart plays her personal assistant, and Assayas uses both of them to delicately and mockingly probe the creative process, performance, aging and female jealousy. Binoche delivers one of her best performances in recent years. The excellent Stewart proves there is life after "Twilight," and Chloë Grace Moretz ("Kick-Ass"), who appears in a guest role, also manages to leave her mark. The result is elegant, enigmatic and thought-provoking, and if you wish, you can see it as the feminine version of "Molière on a Bicycle."

• "Killer Joe": Michael C. Hall ("Dexter"), Sam Shepard and Don Johnson star in a dark and trashy Texas thriller from horror director Jim Mickle (responsible for the American remake of the Mexican cannibal film "We Are What We Are"). A law-abiding family man kills a burglar who broke into his home and finds himself swept into a violent and chilling maelstrom involving corrupt cops, gangsters and snuff films. On paper you've already seen this film before, but Mickle and his regular screenwriter Nick Damici navigate the work in surprising directions. The three leads gleefully commit themselves to the apparently inferior material, and genre fans are sure to leave the theater with a sickly smile.

• "Corn Island": The big winner at the Karlovy Vary Festival is a film festival par excellence. It takes place entirely on a small island in the Mtkvari River that separates Georgia from Abkhazia, has almost no dialogue, and most of its minutes are devoted to methodically following an old man and his granddaughter engaged in agricultural work. Yet if you fancy diving into a fascinating and very special cinematic experience, and you are blessed with a bit more patience than average, "Corn Island" by Giorgi Ovsiannikov, which tells a simple parable about man, nature and eternal political conflicts, is undoubtedly the film for you.

• "Truffaut Forever": Alongside some of the greatest works of legendary French director François Truffaut ("Two English Girls," "Jules and Jim" and "The 400 Blows"), to be screened at the festival marking 30 years since his death, this new documentary, directed by Alexandre Moua, will also be screened. You won't find earth-shattering revelations here, but through old interviews with the great director, perusal of his personal letters and conversations with his friends and colleagues, Moua's delicate, modest and not very long work sketches a moving human portrait of a great filmmaker and awakens a strong desire to watch again the splendid body of his work.

premise_en_haiku45: Lech Wałęsa (Polish: Lech Wałęsa; born September 29, 1943) is a labor union leader, human rights activist, and Polish politician; founder of "Solidarity" (Solidarność), the first independent workers' organization in the Soviet bloc, Nobel Peace Prize laureate (1983), and President of Poland from 1990 to 1995. Wałęsa was born in Popowo, where he studied in elementary and high school until he began working as an electrician at the Lenin Shipyard in Gdańsk (Stocznia Gdańska im. Lenina) in 1967. A year later he married Danuta Wałęsowa, and the couple had eight children. In 1970 he was among the organizers of illegal strikes in the shipyards. Following the violent clashes that ended the strikes, during which over 80 workers were killed by police, he was arrested and convicted of "antisocial behavior," for which he was sentenced to a year in prison. In 1976 he was fired from his job at the shipyards after collecting signatures on a petition to build a monument to the workers killed. Because he was known informally as a "troublemaker," he was unable to find work and supported himself and his family with the help of his friends. In 1978 he was among the founders of the organization Wolne Związki Zawodowe Wybrzeża, an underground and illegal workers' organization. He was arrested several times in 1979 for organizing illegal labor organization, but was found not guilty in his trial and released in early 1980, returning to work at the Gdańsk shipyards. On August 14, 1980, he became the leader of a large strike by shipyard workers, which spread throughout Poland. He convinced the shipyard workers and their colleagues to establish a strike coordination committee (Międzyzakładowy Komitet Strajkowy). In September, the Communist government signed an agreement with the strike coordination committee that permitted legal workers' organization, but not yet a free workers' organization. The committee declared itself such a legal organization, and became the founding committee of "Solidarity," with Wałęsa as chairman. He served in this position until December 1981, when Prime Minister Wojciech Jaruzelski declared martial law. Wałęsa went into hiding in southeastern Poland, near the Soviet border, until November 14, 1982. In 1983 he applied (successfully) to return to work as an electrician at the Gdańsk shipyards; in practice he was under partial house arrest until 1987. In 1983 he was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize, but he did not receive the prize in person, as he feared the Polish government would not allow him to return, so his wife accepted the prize on his behalf and donated the money to the "Solidarity" organization, which was in exile in Brussels. In October 1985 elections were held in Poland, but "Solidarity" boycotted them, claiming that the authorities could not be trusted to conduct them fairly. In November, Jaruzelski resigned as head of government but remained head of the military. In 1988 Wałęsa organized another strike, demanding recognition of "Solidarity" as a legal organization. After 80 days, the government agreed to begin talks, with Wałęsa leading the government's opponents. The results of these talks, called "round table talks," were the restoration of legal status to "Solidarity" and semi-free elections to the Polish parliament. In the 1989 elections, he ran with "Solidarity" as a party and won 48% of the 49% possible (the remaining 51% of parliamentary seats were reserved for the Communist Party, according to the "round table talks"). Although he was only chairman of a workers' organization, Wałęsa played an important role in Polish politics. Toward the end of 1989, he persuaded former Communist leaders to form a coalition government, which became the first non-Communist government in the Soviet bloc. After the coalition was stabilized, parliament elected Tadeusz Mazowiecki as Prime Minister, and Poland began to break away from Communism. At the same time, that year Wałęsa won the Council of Europe Human Rights Prize, along with the Czech Karel Schwarzenberg. On December 9, 1990, Wałęsa was elected President in the Polish presidential election for a term of 5 years. His rule was characterized by frequent changes in government, which drew sharp criticism from across the political spectrum and caused him to lose most of his support by the end of his term. Nevertheless, during his presidency, Poland transformed completely – from a Communist state with a repressive regime under tight Soviet control, into a democratic and free country with a rapidly growing economy. On May 20, 1991, he made an official visit to Israel. This was the first time a Polish president had visited the State of Israel. During the visit he spoke from the Knesset podium and asked for forgiveness from the Jewish people for past events. During the visit he held meetings with President of the State Chaim Herzog, with Prime Minister Yitzhak Shamir, and with the Secretary General of the Histadrut Yisrael Kaiser. Following a meeting with Defense Minister Moshe Arens, he announced the cancellation of a deal for the sale of tanks from Poland to Syria. In the 1995 presidential election, he lost to Alexander Kwaśniewski. In 1995 he established the Lech Wałęsa Institute, a think tank aimed at "documenting the achievements of the Solidarity movement, educating younger generations, promoting democracy and building civil society in Poland and throughout the world." In 1997 he founded a new party, "Christian Democracy of the Third Polish Republic," hoping it would help him succeed in future elections. Wałęsa also ran in the 2000 presidential election, but received less than 1% of the votes. He announced his retirement again and turned to lectures on political history at various universities in Europe. The "Solidarity" movement also failed in parliamentary elections the following year. On May 10, 2004, the name of the international airport of Gdańsk was officially changed to Gdańsk Lech Wałęsa Airport, in recognition of his work. His signature is part of the airport's symbol. In 2006 he left the "Solidarity" movement in protest of its support for the right-wing Law and Justice party led by twins Lech and Jarosław Kaczyński. The main point of contention was the prosecution initiated by the Kaczyński brothers against all those involved in Communist rule and their party's attempt to publish all files of the former Communist secret police. Until then, only members of government and parliament were required to declare any connection with former security services.
