# Gossip

Gossip is conversation whose primary subject matter is other people such as acquaintances, relatives, and celebrities. Gossip involves the dissemination of information that has not received wide publicity, sometimes while infringing on privacy; and generally deals with scandals, topics that fall under the category of malicious speech and schadenfreude. The meaning of the word and the use of the root r-k-l (dissemination of information) in Hebrew were originally entirely negative in ancient times. In modern language, additional meanings have been added to the term. Gossip serves to share and disseminate facts, opinions, and falsehoods equally. Gossip is generally attributed low credibility, and often false facts and fabricated information spread in this way, all intended to arouse false interest in the subjects of conversation. In ancient times, merchants using trade routes would pass news and stories from place to place, and market days were days of encounter between different populations. Peddlers, who wandered with their wares, were the source of sensational news and lively tidings. This is the origin of the word "gossip" or the expression "going about gossiping." These were the same wandering merchants who transmitted both news and "gossip." Today, academic inquiry into gossip focuses on its role in relation to overt and hidden power relations in society. Media outlets, particularly those considered sensationalist, dedicate space to gossip. The pioneer in this field in the State of Israel was journalist Alexander Zauberman, who dedicated considerable space in his newspaper "Special Newspaper" to gossip about the settlement's residents and even included a matchmaking section and jokes in his newspaper. The gossip column of "Ha'olam Hazeh" called "Rachel Spreads Gossip Throughout the World" was usually written by various journalists at the newspaper, based on information brought by Shula Tabor. In its time, this column was considered one of the characteristics of yellow journalism in "Ha'olam Hazeh," but over the years it became a model for gossip columns in Israeli journalism. A later gossip column was "Tzippora," of the newspaper "Chadashot" (after "Chadashot" closed, the section moved to a municipal newspaper), which provided its readers with information such as "Hila Nachshon ex-acy dumb arrived at a party thrown by Itzik Katarza, some dentist in Yokneam. They tried to introduce her to someone, and not long after, the two went out together" (22.9.06). Gossip sections gradually permeated daily newspapers, although even before their establishment, evening newspapers had the practice of publishing society news, including in the section "From Mouth to Ear" which was published in Maariv starting in 1948. Among the journalists who engaged in gossip writing: Gil Meshuali, Gal Ohovsky, Irit Linor, Tzifa Kampinski, Uri Salaai, Shlomi Lauferman, Gabi Amir, Gil Riba, Liora Goldenberg-Stern, and others. In the early nineties, in the supplement "7 Days" of Yedioth Ahronoth, they established the section "Fatal Mission" written by Gabi Amir. In 1997, Gil Riba was appointed as the gossip columnist of the supplement. During his tenure, the section became particularly acerbic and was the terror of celebrities and politicians. To his credit were attributed not a few journalistic exposés that embarrassed the Netanyahu, Barak, and Sharon governments. Riba left the newspaper in 2001; his position was taken over the years by journalists Yigal Bar-Kama, Erik Milman, Yasmin Levi, and Adva Melamet. The grip of gossip columns on Israeli journalism strengthened at the beginning of the 21st century, and thus readers of "Haaretz," which refrained for many years from including a gossip column, can also read about gossip matters concerning prominent figures in the Israeli economic landscape in the TheMarker supplement. Coverage of funerals, particularly of unknowns whom few knew, is an example of a common form of gossip in Israeli media. Gossip is one of the most important informal means of maintaining and reinforcing social norms. Because gossip reveals both norms and the degree of deviation from them, it serves as a value for obtaining information about the social world. Gossip increases group members' loyalty to its values, and ignorance of this increases their anxiety and motivates them to behave in accordance with convention. Gossip serves as a surveillance mechanism also because a person who is part of a group and conveys information about other people to it actually causes him to belong to the group and to be at the center of attention. In fact, one can conclude that people anxious about their place in society tend to spread gossip more than other people in order to be accepted and succeed among their reference groups. Another basic assumption argues that people generally gossip about those who deviated from and violated the accepted social norms of the group. According to this assumption, gossip is in the sense of "social judgment" of those who deviate from the norms. Gossip assists in the transfer of information through which group members learn which behaviors are acceptable and which are not. Gossip constitutes a kind of indirect social sanction against those who deviate from the norms and serves as a warning to a person acting contrary to the accepted code of conduct. Social networks are an effective means of widespread communication connecting many members of a group. Networks allow a much wider range of digital social connections than in the past. For example, Facebook allows an individual to connect with up to 5000 friends from around the world, alongside the ability to participate in Facebook groups and communities and be exposed to people who are not Facebook friends. Thus, people's ability to follow other people through Facebook is greater than in non-virtual space outside the social network. According to Dunbar's number, the larger the discussion group, the greater the tendency for smaller conversations to form within it. Similarly, the ideal number of participants in a discussion is 4 participants. The possibility of creating connections in social networks creates a cross-continental gossip network, and because of this, Facebook constitutes a platform for gossip unlike anything seen before. In the pre-digital era, gossip was part of a practice in which individuals living together and speaking the same language took part, but today gossip has undergone globalization, and it is shared by people from different cultural backgrounds speaking different languages. Greg Atwan and Evan Lushan coin the term "Facebook friend whore" in their book "The Facebook Book" as a criticism of the attempt to create social connections with such a large number of people that cognitively it is not possible for an individual. In the context of gossip, the attempt to create a larger community than is possible for friends influences the behavior of gossip, as it is done regularly, in which groups were smaller. # Falafel or Baguette? Michele Kishka's New Graphic Novel

In a pita or a baguette? Michele Kishka's new graphic novel attempts to tell the story of Israeli "we," while stepping through foundational events • His narrator, an immigrant who fell in love with Israel and longs for what it was, complicates the task from the moment we look at the cover of "Falafel with Hot Sauce," Michele Kishka's new graphic-autobiographical novel, a difference is evident between his new creation and his previous graphic book, "The Second Generation—Things I Didn't Tell Dad" (Modan/Chargol, 2013). If black and white colors adorned the cover of the previous Holocaust novel, which dealt with Kishka's life as the son of a Holocaust survivor, and his figure stood alone on the cover with Auschwitz concentration camp in the background—in "Falafel with Hot Sauce" color dominates. Gray skies are replaced by a bright sky and a crowded celebration of Israeli masses packed on the cover between "Peace Now" signs and "Shabbat" ones. The "I" has been replaced with "we." And what is more the story of the "we" than the book's title, which flutters on the cover? For Kishka, an illustrator, comic and caricature artist, the "general," in this case the story of becoming Israeli and documenting Israeli experience, is always political, serving as a mirror to document a larger social picture steeped in warm humor. What Kishka briefly noted in a paragraph in "The Second Generation," he expands into a full novel: "I decided to leave everything, I came up to the land, was accepted to Bezalel, finished a degree in graphic design, during my studies I met Olivia, we got married and had David."

The book cover opens in the summer of 1969, on his character's first visit to his aunt Paula, sowing the seeds of his love affair in Tel Aviv: "Thirty-five degrees in the shade, the shirt sticks to my body, I feel wonderful." In his European innocence, a foreign child in a candy shop, falafel balls seem to him like meatballs, to which the vendor's generous spoonfuls of spicy liquid are added, which Kishka mistakenly thinks is tomato sauce. That very humorous mistake, illustrated in charming pen, will symbolize Kishka's initial groping and later confident path through Israeli ways. He insists on discovering them despite difficulties of mentality, language, and culture. Frame after frame, square after square, he illustrates Israeli symbols: the choice not to join the Christian Scouting movement like most of his friends in Liaise but to join the Young Guard movement; volunteering on a kibbutz; a Bar Mitzvah celebration a month after the victory of the Six-Day War; a sense of pioneering and mission on journeys throughout the length and breadth of the land; sunrise over Mount Nebo; the first kiss on the farm. The narrator defines this fascination with Israel and the meticulous desire to document his experiences as an irrational, wonderful but not religious love affair. "Holiness is a concept completely foreign to me. I was drawn to physical Israel, not the celestial one," he testifies. That same wonderfulness, his being a "hybrid type, a mixture of two cultures," the abnormality that comprises Israel, "which is in a state of constant warfare but aspires to peace with its neighbors," he expresses through gestures toward surrealist works like "The Treachery of Images" and "The Son of Man" by his countryman, Belgian Magritte, and thus saves that patriotism from banality. The abandonment of socialist values, which cultivate productivity and do not align with Kishka's longing for spiritual life and comic creation ("reactionary and bourgeois," thus members of the movement label the medium in a sentence they deliver to the young artist, who in one of the amusing frames returns to his room to look up the word's meaning in a dictionary) and leaving Kibbutz Ravdim, sharpen one of the central axes around which the novel revolves: pragmatism and productivity. These are expressed in warfare, manual labor, or Kishka's temporary choice of profession in productive and "meaningful" fields, such as architecture. If you will, life versus art. Without the physical ability to fight, Kishka chooses to channel his anger on the stadium walls of Standard Liaise team, on which he writes "Israel will win." Thus, in '74, when he is nineteen, he formally immigrates to the Land of Israel and is drafted for shortened military service, and convinces his commander that it will be more useful to him "with a paintbrush in hand than with an M-16."

When his wife Olivia goes out to "Peace Now" demonstrations, he notes: "Olivia demonstrated for peace and I painted for peace."

Is caricature a central player in culture and its maintenance? Kishka with caricaturist Plantu during his visit to Israel. Photo: Koko

The question of whether political caricature has the power to create and dictate an agenda, and whether it is a central player in the maintenance and development of culture, is woven as a second thread through the novel. If you ask Kishka, a member of "Cartoonists for Peace," founded by his French cartoonist friend Plantu, and in which they fight for freedom of creative expression, the answer echoes yes. The last part, and in my view the most successful in the book, Kishka dedicates at relative length to his work as a political cartoonist and the creative process. He meets cartoonists from around the world, persecuted for their work and the criticism they leveled against their home governments. He illustrates his colleagues and notes the reason for their persecution. Through their stories, no less, the meager Israeli caricature culture is highlighted, especially when Kishka notes his colleagues murdered in the attack on the offices of the satirical newspaper "Charlie Hebdo." Not for nothing does the book end at this point, as if wanting to emphasize the force of the shock, the watershed line that, despite the tragedy inherent in it, does not relax Kishka's hand. Like "The Second Generation," this book also expresses Kishka's talent for building a multi-layered story from places and items of reality; the reader moves with him from one war to another, from the murder of Emil Grunzweig to the assassination of Rabin, one Intifada chasing another, while the round, warm line, almost entirely devoid of black contour, gives the reading experiences cinematic qualities. Aesthetically, the European tradition from which the illustrator draws is evident, maintaining realistic fullness—from illustrating the newspapers of that period, clothing, the red-windowed frame of "Bezalel." It seems the protagonist in this book is aware of his privileged status and does not try to hide it, perhaps even proud of it. The veteran lecturer, who raised generations of illustrators, mourns that he has become an archaeological fossil, a secular and leftist Jew, an "extinct species" in his phrasing. He illustrates himself compressed in formaldehyde like a laboratory animal. It seems that at times the quality of the illustrations surpasses the strength of the words, and they appear as decoration to the visuals or fail in cliché. This is evident, for example, when Olivia is wounded at the demonstration in which Grunzweig is murdered, and her "scar healed over time but the tear in Israeli society remains gaping," or when the protagonist declares: "God is quite a DJ who wants everyone on the dance floor." The choice to create an illustrated account that purports to cover more than 30 years, rather than focus on an event or focused memory, is sometimes against the book's grain. Kishka said in an interview that he deliberately aimed at readers across the sea as well, and it shows. This is because Kishka's protagonist often seems like a satisfied bourgeois yearning for a period that will never return. Also the choice not to divide the book into chapters (unlike "The Second Generation") creates a sense of excess and quick passage between events. And yet, it is an original, important, and groundbreaking work. One might wonder why graphic-historical novels are absent from Israeli bookshelves, and why there is an almost immediate tendency for Israeli comic creators to only deal with "here and now." In addition to Kishka's audacity, the book provides a loving, compassionate, funny, and despairing mirror of Israelis.

# Survivor: Everyone Against Everyone

The public auction arrived just in time to show us that from now on it's every survivor for themselves • Coming soon: our bets on the finale • Episodes 44-45 on Matcha

Friends, we're excited to announce - the finale is around the corner. Of course, by "around the corner" we mean you still need to travel dozens more hours through an endless stream of mind-numbing events, take a turn at the "Villa of the Eliminated," stop at "Big Disputes Square," and get stuck at dozens of special traffic lights on the way to the finale. In short, despite there already being an estimated date, there's still a long way to go, and during which, judging by the promo, the survivors will manage to switch alliances like socks. We're in any case starting to bet on who makes it to the finale, but we'll save that for a separate column, if you don't mind.

## A New Era

In Tuesday's episode, the survivors are also starting to smell the finale - Assi is displaying an outward demeanor of calm, but internally he's already divvying up the jury votes. It's not good for him to reach the finale with his allies, since they're actually the ones who could vote for him as jurors, while continuing his competition with them will be a struggle for jury votes already eliminated. They ate from the same trough and that's it.

Assi made a clever and rather surprising move and turned to form an alliance with Eden. The fact that he initiated it perhaps makes him more "dirty," but it's a strategically brilliant move and Eden the tycoon understands this too and was happy to cooperate. This is double risk, because beyond the fact that they need to eliminate their friends delicately so the jurors don't turn against them, they're now dependent on each other's mercy. Assi didn't hesitate to betray his friends in the past, and Eden might still surprise.

In the negotiation hut, Alina befriends herself with her feelings, and gives us another gaping mouth, discovering that she needs to eat a huge bowl of peanut butter to beat Ragev. On the agenda - a conversation with Rafael Chavibi (father of), who understands that Alina's staying will help Eden more and decides to encourage her specifically. Ragev also doesn't seem eager to win the challenge, and Alina scores a first and significant victory.

## Survivor: Island Wretches

## Survivor: What If?

But does the alliance situation get shaken up again like a sponge? Because here Jordan turns to Assi and offers him... wait, what did she offer him? It was something like "I won't leave my alliance and you won't leave yours, but I enjoy watching you play and maybe we'll do something." We didn't understand - do you want to exercise together? Sign up for a macramé class? Join "Bozglos"? Bottom line, Jordan wanted to go and feel free, and Assi gently waved her off, just like a Tinder chat where it's clear it's going nowhere and the other side says "we'll talk tomorrow," really meaning "let's pretend this never happened."

Let's jump ahead to the next duel challenge, which Alina entered skipping. Pier - despite barely seeing her five minutes - we missed her. After Ragev gets irritated for a moment over the word "twisted" ("Why twisted? What did I twist?"), Alina decides to continue their riveting romance and takes him on another challenge. Against the backdrop of a recently published interview with past survivor Omer Rozen, who spoke about how the production wanted competitors' praise, received immunity challenges that seem tailored to their measurements, it's hard not to wonder if this challenge too is at least comfortable for Alina, the dancer with strong stability. Unsurprisingly, she wins and takes Ragev's vote, causing a flip in votes and now Eden and Jordan's alliance is leading.

## Eating the Cake and Keeping It Whole

Saturday's episode opens with Ella's sad confession about struggling to form meaningful connections with girls throughout her life, and we promise if she didn't get a nasty sentence toward someone in the coming episodes, we might start liking her. But never mind - the main course in this episode is the public auction challenge, which is always fun to watch.

A moment before - the social ranking that's not really relevant to anyone except the one ranked last. In this case it's as expected Beni, who was denied participation. Pier, there's nothing worse than that.

We won't mention all the packages, but here are some moments we especially loved:

**The nicest moment:** The "player card" that Eden Chavibi bought, allowing him to either bring Beni into the game or get extra money for himself. Eden of course chooses the friendly/smart strategic move to include Beni in the game. While Israel was quick to bite at the fact that it's all strategy in the food chain, and that Eden doesn't really love Beni, hey - immediately after that karma gave Eden a slap. There's justice in the world.

**The funniest moment:** In this case it's every single one of Ragev's purchases, where Gia kept giving him the chance to swap the package he chose for another, and he kept staying with his choices, until the moment when the weak one lifted and he discovered "essential" items like Botox injections and dental floss. And we thought Beni was the comic character of the season.

**The most-actually-funniest moment:** But with all due respect to Ragev's blunders, Ella fell big into Gia's trap when he announced a package that makes him do rotational movements. And this after she won the useful "makeup-hair" package, right? She sent 650 pesos toward Gia and squealed toward him in joy, but when the weak one was lifted it turned out to be a picture of hummus and not the real thing. "How could you do this to me?" she blurted out in offense, and after the sense of discomfort passed over us, we had to be lifted off the floor from laughing.

**The most delicious moment:** Jordan waited and waited and at some point it became annoying - where's your sportsmanship? But like in competitions against a tough female judoka from a foreign country, Jordan knew exactly what she was doing. She waited for the right moment, and then when the package that caught her attention arrived, there weren't many competitors left and Jordan managed to buy two enormous portions - pitas and a platter of salads, and a roll with sausage plus beer. The beer is to hide your eyes from the other survivors. Still, how delicious - it's not that pleasant.

**The most horrifying moment:** In the final minutes of the episode, when it was already clear the challenge was about to end, Beni offered to buy the cake for everyone, and the merciful and gracious Gia agreed to provide a happy ending to today's episode, and called Ella to take the cake and serve everyone. Mmm, while she's walking toward the survivors with the cake she dipped a finger in the cake to taste, began to slip and for one horrible moment the cake began to slide and almost fell. Lucky that Ella managed to straighten herself in time. In the end she still mumbled "I'm okay." Bottom line, there are courses that could go down the drain.

Finally, let's comment on the change of name to the promo that in direct continuation of the previous episode's events presents the renewed tribe division plan. So, according to the promo (and only according to it, yes?), Assi tries to pull Beni back to them while Ragev might join Jordan altogether. We're actually not at all sure any of these moves actually happened, but one thing's for sure - the next eliminations will get as dramatic as we get closer to the finale. After all, a million shekels.

Beni: "If he's laughing without me even throwing a single punch, that's it guys, I'm in the right profession"

Gia: "Actually from your punches I'm not laughing" (Let's see you, Mister Host #2)

"Gia, can you register me until the land?" (Ragev, clarifying if the public auction is also in the surrounding area)

# From Shopping Mall to Consumer Purchases to Business Operations

## The Digital Revolution Forcing Traditional Malls to Change

Massive online shopping is eating away at stores and pushing malls to take on new forms. One creative and original direction is transforming them into service malls for businesses.

In recent years, we are witnessing a change in consumption habits throughout the world. Malls are emptying out, some are closing, and large chains are weakening and earning much less thanks to direct online shopping. Traditional malls are being replaced by online stores that offer a very wide variety of products at much lower prices without needing to leave home. Are we approaching the disappearance of malls? If you ask Elad Dar, an entrepreneur and businessman, he would answer you very clearly—they are not going to disappear, they will simply change. Meet the Israeli businessman who is establishing the first mall that will provide comprehensive solutions for business owners and professionals.

Elad Dar (41) from Tel Aviv left school at age 16 and a half, to his parents' dismay. In conversation with him, he tells of the big dreams he had since his youth. "I told them I wanted to be independent, even though they thought I was going in a completely different direction. You could say not everyone believed I would succeed. At age 20, I had a company that provided services to lawyers, with messengers throughout the country. At 23, I moved from Nesher Ziona to Tel Aviv, rented an office, and almost went bankrupt. I immediately realized I had no idea how to run a business despite all my big dreams. I understood that I had to consult with experts and learn properly how to manage my life's enterprise. So I decided to get business consulting, and within five months my business grew six times over. Right after the success, I decided I also wanted to study business consulting. At that time, I opened another company and both companies ran on their own, money flowed, and I became specialized."

## "I Promised I Would Stay in Israel"

Dar's success continued and within just five years he turned the school where he studied into an international success. "After I finished my studies in 2006, I decided to open a business consulting company called SUCCESS. In 2009, I had a shortage of manpower and simply bought the college where I studied business consulting, Herbert College. Thanks to the tools I acquired in my studies, I managed to leverage my acquisition, and in 2011 I started lecturing around the world on methods I had developed. A year later, I opened the first college branch in the Czech Republic, and within three years, 15 branches opened in many countries around the world, including Holland, Germany, and the United States."

Beyond being a successful businessman, he had a dream. Elad was a father to four sons and always dreamed of a daughter. His wife, who had dealt with raising children while he spent considerable time abroad on business, made bringing another child conditional on his staying in Israel to work. Elad agreed, and so it was.

"At that time, something else happened—I had four sons born to me," he says. "My wife told me it was hard for her that I was always abroad and she had to raise the children alone. The big difficulty came when I asked for another child. I really wanted a daughter, so I promised her I would stay in Israel, and so it was. My wife became pregnant and our little daughter Nia was born to us. So after I consulted for many people and helped them make their businesses succeed, it was time for me to invest in myself.

"Now, after choosing to stay and work in Israel, I decided to establish the first business mall in the world. I thought about it about ten years ago but didn't have the money to make the idea happen. Now it's happening and in a big way."

## What Exactly Is a Business Mall?

"It's a unique model like no other—a building where professionals provide services to businesses. The mall is limited to two professionals in each field. The idea is to provide business owners and professionals in Israel with a range of all service providers. There are rooms called 'New York' and 'Wall Street.'"

"Every month there is a networking meeting for all the tenants."

"It's a mall where every client who enters it is a client of all the shop owners in the mall. For example, a business owner needs the services of a lawyer, graphic designer, content writer, accountant, and other services. Here I bring them all together into one large, sophisticated business mall. The building is equipped with the most advanced technology so that anyone in the building will get work just by being in the building. The mall itself will provide all the services to business owners."

## "A Lot of Courage and Faith"

Elad's vision is that clients of one of the building's clients will become clients of all the others. There are two professionals from each field so the client can compare work quality and prices, and thus can get solutions for all their needs in one place.

"The client must have a choice option, and therefore I chose to allow more than one professional from each field to work in the business mall," he explains. "Beyond the fact that everyone is in the same compound, the entire building is equipped with a smart television system that allows every guest in the building to be exposed to other service providers in the building. Throughout the building there are televisions with advertisements of other service providers. The televisions direct guest traffic to other rooms, and everywhere in the building there are screens that guide clients so that it is very rare for a client to miss the service providers in the mall. It's a WIN-WIN situation. The client will get all the services in one place, and business owners in the mall will get clients. The building is equipped with a telephone system that connects business owners so they can also communicate with each other easily."

And what do business owners in your building gain when they refer to another service provider?

"Here comes another advantage. We developed a special app with our virtual coins. For every referral from one service provider to another service provider, they will enjoy benefits, and so I'm actually encouraging a tenant to send clients to another tenant. The currency is called MEDIX. The idea is to reward those who refer from one to another. At the same time, we developed a unique app for the building. Anyone who comes to the building will be able to receive a booking that identifies them as a guest, and the app is the permanent entry card. There's an option to mark arrival at several businesses, and every tenant who brought a client to the building receives additional MEDIX."

## "The Virtual Currency of the Building"

"The virtual currency of the building allows building tenants to enjoy free advertising. The more virtual coins a client has, the more they can enjoy discounts and free advertising in the mall and in the business mall's newsletter. Not only service providers in the mall enjoy benefits—clients who come to the mall do too. Guests who come to the building also enjoy lotteries that will encourage them to come and visit the mall. The lotteries will be conducted through the app, and so we're actually encouraging guests to come and receive the services of the building's tenants. Beyond that, there's also the option to chat with any of the building's tenants via chat in the app and at the same time ask a general question that will reach all service providers in the building."

## Now for the Interesting Part—How Much Will It Cost for a Professional to Enter the Business Mall?

"This is the best part—the price is 3,000 shekels for an office, including furniture and all other services. The price is affordable and fair for every business owner, even for new businesses. We don't have shareholders and people who need to take a bite out of profits. It's just me with a lot of courage and faith in my venture. I've invested everything I have in this building, and I'm sure it's going to help many business owners."

"The services they will receive are a photography studio, meeting rooms, coffee capsules at no extra charge, a phone line including a thousand minutes of calls for every office, professional business consulting included in the price. Every month there is a networking meeting for all the tenants. My mission is to help business owners, and this will happen very soon. The structure is in advanced stages of construction and starting in May it will begin operating."

## "Everyone Helps Everyone"

Elad is targeting all business owners, beginners and those who have been in the market for many years. "Everyone comes to us. There are small new companies alongside large companies, and everyone helps everyone. That's the whole idea. It's like an advanced community that will help every service provider in the mall get clients. The low monthly cost equals advertising at the same amount on any other platform. We're simply helping them get new clients. Will the traditional mall as we know it today disappear soon? Elad has a very interesting answer."

"Today everyone is on the internet. Regular malls are going to die. When you want a service from a business owner, you sit with them and don't talk to them on the internet. Everything is changing, and service providers will be the new malls. Clothes and fashion are moving to the internet. Costs are decreasing, and you can see this very clearly in the trend of recent years. Giant chains are leaving Israel, and we're already in negotiations to bring SUCCESS CENTER to regular malls as well. The first business mall opening in May will be the first. It will happen in Tel Aviv, and the horizon looks very interesting in this whole field. Additional surprises are expected."

## Tips from a Businessman Who Crossed the Ocean

As a businessman who crossed the ocean and succeeded in many countries around the world, Elad has a few tips for the beginning entrepreneur.

"The most important thing is to know where you're bringing your clients from. If someone who opens a business doesn't know for sure where their traffic is coming from, then it's not worth anything. First of all, it's important to know where you're bringing clients and work from. If advertising costs exceed income, then it's not worth anything anymore."

For our purposes, let's assume the value is 10 meters per second squared. If we are at 2g, we are actually accelerating at approximately 20 meters per second squared. Most people begin to feel dizzy and even blurred vision due to oxygen deprivation reaching the brain at 4g. This is why amusement park rides (like roller coasters for example) remain within this range of acceleration.

The force acting on a pilot or a person on a roller coaster consists of two components: Earth's gravitational force, which always points toward the center of the Earth, and an additional force resulting from the acceleration of the vehicle itself. The second force is actually a fictitious force because it does not result from pushing or the action of another body.

G-forces acting on pilots:

A pilot in a plane accelerating upward at an acceleration of 5g will feel 5 g-forces downward as a result of the acceleration plus one additional g-force due to his weight, meaning a total of 6 g-forces. The pilot will be pushed forcefully toward the seat and will actually feel the pressure the seat exerts back on him. The pilot will feel 6 times heavier than normal and will even have difficulty raising his arms. In this situation there is a physiological danger because the force acts on the blood downward, preventing blood flow to the brain, which is why the pilot can lose consciousness. Without using g-suits and training, a pilot can lose consciousness after about five seconds under 6 g-forces. G-suits apply pressure to the pilot's legs and abdomen, actually pushing blood back to the brain. Using these suits, pilots can avoid losing consciousness even when subjected to 9 g-forces.

As mentioned, the total g-force acting on a pilot is the downward gravitational force and the fictitious force acting in the direction opposite to the plane's acceleration. # G-Force Explained

The 'g-force' on a body is its acceleration relative to free fall. We use the term 'force' in this context because such accelerations are not created by gravity itself, but result from other types of forces that cause pressure and tension on bodies. G-force is not directly related to Earth's gravitational force. Generally, in engineering applications, gravitational acceleration g can also help define a unit of measurement for force. As we know, weight is the gravitational force acting on a body and its magnitude is the body's mass multiplied by gravitational acceleration (mg). Therefore, g-force can be thought of as a unit of force measurement, defined such that a body's weight equals a force of 1g. If we say, for example, that 2 g-forces are acting, we actually mean the force intensity is the body's mass times 2g, that is, 2mg. Measurement of 'g-forces' is done using an accelerometer. As mentioned, the term 'g-force' is a misnomer. It is actually the acceleration a mass experiences in a particular situation. On Earth, 1g is approximately 9.8 meters per second squared. For our purposes, let's assume the value is 10 meters per second squared. If we are at 2g, we are actually accelerating at approximately 20 meters per second squared. Most people begin to feel dizzy and even blurred vision due to oxygen deprivation reaching the brain at 4g. This is why amusement park rides (like roller coasters for example) remain within this range of acceleration.

The force acting on a pilot or a person on a roller coaster consists of two components: Earth's gravitational force, which always points toward the center of the Earth, and an additional force resulting from the acceleration of the vehicle itself. The second force is actually a fictitious force because it does not result from pushing or the action of another body.

G-forces acting on pilots:

A pilot in a plane accelerating upward at an acceleration of 5g will feel 5 g-forces downward as a result of the acceleration plus one additional g-force due to his weight, meaning a total of 6 g-forces. The pilot will be pushed forcefully toward the seat and will actually feel the pressure the seat exerts back on him. The pilot will feel 6 times heavier than normal and will even have difficulty raising his arms. In this situation there is a physiological danger because the force acts on the blood downward, preventing blood flow to the brain, which is why the pilot can lose consciousness. Without using g-suits and training, a pilot can lose consciousness after about five seconds under 6 g-forces. G-suits apply pressure to the pilot's legs and abdomen, actually pushing blood back to the brain. Using these suits, pilots can avoid losing consciousness even when subjected to 9 g-forces.

Negative g-forces:

As mentioned, the total g-force acting on a pilot is the downward gravitational force and the fictitious force acting in the direction opposite to the plane's acceleration. The magnitude of the fictitious force depends on acceleration and can be much stronger than the gravitational force. If the plane accelerates strongly downward, upward g-forces will act on it. In such circumstances this will cause increased blood flow to the brain. This situation is very dangerous (perhaps more dangerous than blood deprivation to the brain). It is known that humans have lower tolerance to g-forces acting upward than tolerance to positive g-forces. A person generally cannot withstand a force of 3g upward for more than a few seconds.

Note: If the plane is in free fall, the plane's acceleration actually equals Earth's gravitational acceleration, and therefore no g-forces act on the pilot at all. Such a situation occurs for astronauts in a space shuttle, as it is in a state of free fall.

# A State of Halakha or Halakha of the State?

Why is the domain of commandments and religious laws called "halakha"? What is the meaning of the names in the Book of Ruth? And what is Meir Ariel's solution?

The term "halakha state" returned to public discourse this week, following statements by Bezalel Smotrich. Beyond the ideological debate, there is also an interesting linguistic question: why is the broad domain of commandments and religious laws called "halakha"? What is the connection between the verb of movement "to go" and laws and commandments?

The answer leads to one of the prominent characteristics of the Hebrew language: figurativeness—the transfer of terms, words, and expressions from the physical domain to the abstract domain. In this case, the verb of movement "to go" and words from the root h-l-k undergo a transition from the physical domain to the domain of speech, thought, and belief.

"Halakha" is a very common Talmudic word. In Pirkei Avot it is written: "One who learns from his fellow one chapter, or one halakha, or one verse, or one saying, or even one letter, should treat him with honor."

The Mishnah and Talmud are full of "halakhot" in varying degrees of severity, but the source for this can already be found in the Bible. There are very many verbs from the root h-l-k—over 1,500—and most are related to movement, but some of them deal with the fulfillment of commandments. A few examples, each with additional versions:

"And you shall keep My statutes to walk in them" (Leviticus 18:4)

"To walk in His ways and to keep His commandments" (Deuteronomy 30:16)

"He walked in the statutes of life" (Ezekiel 33:15)

"In the path of righteousness I walk" (Proverbs 8:20)

"The way that the Lord your God has led you" (Deuteronomy 8:2)

The idea is simple: fulfilling commandments is walking in a path that has been marked out by some authority, and yet there is within it a measure of dynamism and flexibility. Alongside this, the word "halikh" (gait) is used in the Book of Job to mean leg. In modern Hebrew, the word acquired a new meaning: legal proceedings, divorce proceedings. The word "halikhot" means manner of behavior, in the phrase "customs and manners," which already appears in the Bible: "She watches over the ways of her household" (Proverbs 31:27) and "The everlasting ways are His" (Habakkuk 3:6).

Other verbs of movement tell the same story. "To conduct" is in the Bible, as it is today, a verb of movement from which words such as "custom" and "manner" were born in the sources, along with the verb "to behave." "To proceed" means to advance by walking, and from this come management and also "manual" in modern Hebrew. And from the human leg came the words "habit," "accustomed," "to accustom," and "exercise." They are all related to behavior and not to physical movement.

Here lies the difference between "halakha" and "commandment" or "law." A commandment is halakha frozen in place; it emphasizes hierarchy rather than dynamic action. Law is what is engraved in stone, something that cannot be changed. "A halakha state" is somewhat of a linguistic oxymoron. A "state" is an institution or government capable of establishing judgment and law. "Halakha" is a dynamic system, rich with disputes and struggles among "halakha decisors." It is entrusted to rabbis within the framework of religious communities, and there it should remain.

# Orpah, Who Turned Her Back on Her Mother-in-Law

In honor of the holiday of Shavuot, Uri Heitner presents an interesting perspective related to the Book of Ruth: "What immediately catches the eye is the names of the heroes of the text, which practically invite midrashic interpretation:

Elimelech: "He was saying: 'To me shall kingship come'" (Midrash Ruth Rabbah). A hint in the metrics about information regarding the continuation of the dynasty, which will be transmitted at the end of the scroll—David is a descendant of the family.

Naomi: "Her deeds were pleasant and pleasing" (Midrash Ruth Rabbah).

Mahlon and Chilion: "Mahlon—because he was smitten from the world; Chilion—because he perished from the world" (Midrash Ruth Rabbah). One can also interpret the name Mahlon as a person who dies from illness. To this we should add a midrash from the Talmud Bavli, in Tractate Bava Batra: "And why were they called Mahlon and Chilion? Mahlon—because they made their bodies unhealthy; Chilion—because they were punished with destruction before the Almighty."

Orpah and Ruth: "Orpah, who turned her back on her mother-in-law... Ruth, who heeded her mother-in-law's words."

Ruth: "Rabbi Yochanan said: Why was she called Ruth? Because she merited and David came from her, whom the Holy One, blessed be He, rewarded with songs and praises" (Yalkut Shimoni, Ruth). Another midrash—Ruth = companions.

# From Virtual Cheerfulness to Visual Mischief

In July we will mark 20 years since the untimely death of Meir Ariel. In preparation for the event, his family published a book containing texts Ariel wrote over the years, edited by Atura Opak. The name of the book, like one of Ariel's songs: "The Doctor of Cleverness (He Really Knew How to Die...)." To mark the book's publication, a special evening was held last week at the artist's studio.

Ariel's texts complement the versatility of this special man, this wise and charming rabbi. In my view, as presented on the Linguistic Arena website, Meir Ariel is a language hero, and in the realm of language in Israeli music he is the greatest of all. The book contains many genres: letters, eulogies, stories, humorous sketches, and more. In some of them, Ariel naturally addresses language itself, and in others he plays with it. Here are some examples.

What is Israeli language: "The coolest cocktail party, and one business, avant communicative, and then assertive, smooth gentility, hyper-active, overlapping super, celebrity snobbish, small talk slick, bullshit basically, intellectual-schmintellectual, fine online, a comeback bouncer, innate scheming, outish vulgarity, a postmodern charter, from virtual cheerfulness, visual mischief, hello—hey, yalla—bye." (From the book "The Israelis" by Micha Kirshenblatt, 1997).

Meir's vision: "Behold, days are coming and people will lose the taste of escape, and masks will be removed and there will be confession of truth. Beliefs and opinions and outlooks will be cast away and people will confess to mistakes and adopt new beliefs, open to negotiation. All known institutions and mechanisms will disintegrate and disappear, and refined systems of government open to negotiation will be established in their place. Behold, days are coming." (1990s).

Explanations fractured by desires and runnings: "The Book of Explanations is a book of the root r-tz-h and t-r-tz, which generates will and satisfaction, to please and to satisfy, which generate explanations in the home, in the courtroom, in the study hall, and in every place and matter that there is a mouth to argue, to provide an explanation, so that the ear is pleased and satisfied... The Book of Explanations does not deal with the roots r-tz and r-tz-tz, whose sound is similar in various declensions and close to the root of explanations and desires. I wanted to please you with fractured explanations. This is a book of a presentation of explanations explained to the satisfaction of the observer to find favor in the eyes of the reader, so that all are pleased and satisfied." (Book of Explanations, 1998).

On the laundry of words: "I bless the section called 'Word Laundry,' in which I found a partner in the anxiety that sometimes grips me in the face of the wandering of words from their meaning to a different meaning, though not with the sharpness of the examples you brought, but with the same degree of danger. For example, 'the lion spreads his wings,' 'the lion took off,' and there are 'young lion' and 'jackal,' and you're not sure if a lion will remain to practice medicine to rule over the beasts." (Letter to David Grossman following "The Yellow Time," 1987).

On the culture of discourse in the kibbutz: "As is known, every speech at the general assembly begins with the word: 'Comrades!' and before the speaker takes a breath for the second sentence of his speech, the comrades hurry to show him how truly comrades they are: they burst forth, split, interject things irrelevant to the matter. A thing that drags them all into a whirlpool where everything in it, except what should really be there, exists." (Sermon at a kibbutz assembly, 1980s).

On Naomi Shemer: "Naomi Shemer—for the shivers of pleasantness... Naomi Zamer—for the shivers of Hasidic melodies... Naomi Tzmer—for pleasant shivers... Naomi Gamer—for shivers in melodies." (Upon Naomi Shemer's winning the Israel Prize, 1983).

On Nathan Alterman: "For stars in swaddling clothes. A squirrel on the shoulders of the forest. The milk of the inn. The ends of the roads are only longing. What positive-negative current runs-bounces like on embers: in fire (negative), kisses (positive), the mouth (positive) which is torn (negative) to call (positive) to the earth (positive) that (negative) homeland (positive)... Alterman's scar—sound, weight, rhythm, melody, brightness, thought—did not leave me for years." (Stations of influence and inspiration in my life, 1995).

On men of action, poor in spirit: "So stop already talking all the time in the tone of five-six-ton-apples-per-dunam, or in the tone of cubic-meter-per-hour, or in the tone of concrete. And raise your eyes a bit, which look only downward all the time, measuring only your height, yes: raise your eyes also around you—there is space... above you—there is height... maybe you'll see some hovering sparkle... some spirit man signaling... maybe you'll even be ashamed, you men of action." (Main title, 1986).

# The Child Who Lived in a Balagan

Several responses came following the discussion of the multilingual word "balagan." Rafi Ashet writes: "Balagan means tent in Russian. I told an old friend (93) and he remembered, that 48 years ago they were in tents, and a Russian mother came to visit her son and said to him: 'Oh, you live in a balagan.'"

Esther Samueli writes: "To the balakhan-balkhan-balagan one can add the Balkan mountains and countries, whose etymology according to researchers is identical to that of the former." It turns out this is indeed so. Researchers are divided on the origin of the name Balkan, which means in Turkish 'chain of wooded mountains.' Similar words are found in various Turkish languages, but the origin leads to Persian. Some believe the origin is in 'balak-mod' which means swampy forest. Another opinion is that the origin of Balkan is indeed in bala-khana in Persian, which means high and large house, and it is also the origin of balagan.

# I Traveled to Harmi'el with a Nun and Clay

Sigal writes: "I wish to consult, or more precisely to deliberate, regarding the proper vocalization of certain words in standard form. In your opinion, is there room in certain texts to make exceptions to the rule, and this for reasons of preserving sound? For example, to vocalize the verb 'to pickpocket' as such, instead of the standard form 'to pickpocket.'

For the non-standard form sounds much more natural and friendly, and despite its lack of standardness, it does not sound too harsh as does the standard form, or when the linguistic-social situation in the book requires non-standard pronunciation. I would be happy to hear your opinion."

The issue is much broader than certain verbs. The laws of begad-kefet are implemented in a very partial way in spoken language. Netiva Ben-Yehuda defined the phenomenon when she scolded Dalia Mazor who spoke about "a film about a nun and clay," when of course she meant a nun and a priest.

No resident of the Galilean city would say he is "traveling to Harmi'el," and another would go to Petach Tikva not to Petah Tikva, and certainly not to Poland. Nevertheless, in many cases the rules are preserved even in spoken language. To spoil and not to spoil, to cook and not to cook, and so on. In the realm of the verb, it appears the main problems are with verbs beginning with the consonant k.

And regarding the question, the issue naturally arises only in vocalized texts, and these are generally aimed at books of poetry and children's books. In these, despite sometimes being foreign, it is important to maintain normative vocalization, and deviate from it only when dealing with spoken dialogue. Most texts are not vocalized and the problem does not exist. On the other hand, in free speech excessive adherence to the rules creates foreignness, and it is better to preserve it for cases where precise pronunciation is required.

# The Observable Universe

In cosmology, the observable universe contains the galaxies and other matter that we can in principle observe now from Earth, because light from distant objects has taken time to reach us since the expansion of the universe. A distinction must be made between the "universe" and the "observable universe." Assuming the universe is isotropic, the distance to the edge of the observable universe is generally the same in all directions. That is, the observable universe has a spherical volume with the observer at its center, regardless of the shape of the universe as a whole (isotropy means that the laws of physics are the same in all directions in the universe). At every location in the universe there is its own observable universe, which may or may not overlap with "our" observable universe, with Earth at its center.

Electrons scatter radiation very efficiently, but radiation in the young universe could not travel freely; in fact, the young universe was opaque to radiation. As the universe continued to expand, it cooled to approximately 3,000 degrees Kelvin, and at this point hydrogen atoms formed. That is, protons and electrons combined. At this stage of the universe, radiation could spread and scatter. Why? Because at this stage most electrons were trapped inside hydrogen atoms, and therefore radiation could travel freely and scatter until today... According to this theory of the Big Bang, this radiation is the cosmic microwave background. The background radiation actually provides a snapshot of the universe at that time. This time is called the last scattering surface, when radiation last scattered off electrons and protons. The term "observable" does not depend on whether technological means allow detection of radiation from any object in that region. The word "observable" simply indicates that in principle there is a possibility for light to reach us (Earth) from an object in the universe.

In practice, we can see objects not far from the last scattering surface, up until shortly after the universe was no longer opaque to photons. An image of the observable universe as observed by the Hubble Telescope. Each point is a galaxy containing billions of stars.

The age of the universe is approximately 13.7 billion years, but due to the expansion of the universe, we now observe objects that are currently at a distance far greater than the static distance of 13.7 billion light-years. Per Håkan Gessle (Swedish: Per Håkan Gessle; born January 12, 1959) is a Swedish singer, songwriter, and guitarist. He is best known for his role in the Swedish pop rock band Roxette, which he founded together with Marie Fredriksson in 1986 and which disbanded following her death in 2019. The band achieved enormous international success in the late 1980s and early 1990s with their album Look Sharp! released in 1988 and their album Joyride released in 1991, which contained songs that topped the American music charts four times, including the particularly successful song "It Must Have Been Love," which was also included in the soundtrack to the film Pretty Woman. Before founding Roxette, Gessle had a successful career in Sweden as a member of the band Hep Stars, which released three albums that reached number one on Sweden's album charts in the early 1980s, but the band broke up shortly after their fourth album, The Heartland Café, released in 1984. Over the years, Gessle has also recorded many solo albums, both in Swedish and English. After Fredriksson's health deteriorated in 2002, Gessle released the album Mazarin in 2003. The album was commercially successful, and as a result, a long-term collaboration began between him and backing vocalist Helena Josefsson. After Fredriksson recovered, he created three additional studio albums with her - "Son of a Plumber" in 2005, "En händig man" in 2007, and "Party Crasher" in 2008. After Roxette's world tour ended in 2015, Gessle produced three solo albums - "En vacker natt" in 2017, "En vacker dag" in 2017, and "Small Town Talk" in 2018. In 2016, Gessle began releasing several singles under the fictitious stage name Mono Mind, and in 2019 he released the studio album "Mind Control" under this stage name. Gessle is the primary songwriter for the bands Roxette and Hep Stars. Gessle was born in 1959 in the city of Hälmstad in Sweden. Per Gessle was a founding member of the band Hep Stars, which was founded in 1976. The band quickly became popular in Sweden, but ultimately in 1984 the band disbanded after their fourth album, The Heartland Café, did not achieve commercial success comparable to the band's other albums. In 1982, Gessle released his first solo album "Per Gessle," and after Hep Stars disbanded, he released his second album "Scener" in 1985. Gessle and Marie Fredriksson were friends for several years before they decided to found the band Roxette together in 1986. After the success of their first hit "Neverending Love," written by Gessle, they recorded the album "Pearls of Passion" using material originally intended for Per's third solo album. Roxette went on to bring four singles to number one on the American music charts and two singles to number two on the American music charts with the albums Look Sharp! released in 1988 and Joyride released in 1991. Following Roxette's success in the early 1990s, Gessle released a demo album in 1992 with a collection of songs. After the band released the album Crash! Boom! Bang! and after the band's subsequent world tour, the band decided to take a break. In 1996, after the band Hep Stars reunited and held a tour, Gessle recorded his first solo album in English. In 2005, Gessle released the solo album "Son of a Plumber," which contained songs in English and several collaborations with other Swedish artists including Jens Jansson, Josefsson, and Lundqvist. The album, which was released in November 2005, also contained a song dedicated to his father, who was a plumber. In Sweden, the album quickly became a platinum record and achieved impressive success in Germany. However, it did not become a hit internationally. This was the first time in eight years that they had performed together on the same stage. He had an older brother named Bengt and an older sister named Gunilla. In 1993, Gessle married Asa Nordin. The couple has one son born on August 5, 1997. " בכל חודש יש מפגש נטוורקינג לכל הדיירים" "מדובר בקניון שכל לקוח שנכנס לתוכו הוא לקוח של כל בעלי החנויות בקניון לדוגמה, בעל עסק צריך שירותים של עורך דין, גרפיקאי, כותב תוכן, רואה חשבון ושירותים נוספים, כאן אני מאגד את כולם יחד לקניון עסקי אחד גדול ומשוכלל. הבניין מרושת בטכנולוגיה המתקדמת ביותר כך שכל מי שנמצא בבניין יקבל עבודה מעצם היותו בבניין, הקניון עצמו יספק את כל השירותים לבעלי העסקים". "הצרכן הישראלי אוהב איכות וטריות, אבל גם רגיש למחיר. הוא מעדיף לבקר פיזית בסופרמרקטים, דבר שנתפס בעיניו כחוויה" "המטבע הווירטואלי של הבניין מאפשר לדיירי הבניין ליהנות מפרסום בחינם, ככל שיש ללקוח יותר מטבעות וירטואליים שכאלה הוא יוכל ליהנות מהנחות ופרסום בחינם בבניין ובניוזלטר של הקניון העסקי. לא רק נותני השירות בקניון נהנים מהטבות, גם הלקוחות שמגיעים לקניון. אורחים שמגיעים לבניין נהנים גם מהגרלות שיעודדו אותם להגיע ולבקר בקניון, ההגרלות יעשו באמצעות האפליקציה וכך בעצם אנחנו מעודדים אורחים להגיע ולקבל את שירותי הדיירים בבניין. מעבר לכך ישנה גם אפשרות לשוחח עם כל אחד מדיירי הבניין בצ'אט באפליקציה ובמקביל להעלות שאלה כללית שתפנה לכל נותני השירות בבניין". ועכשיו למה שמעניין במה, כמה יעלה לבעל מקצוע להיכנס לקניון העסקי ומה הוא מקבל בעבור השכירות החודשית? "השירותים שהם יקבלו הם סטודיו לצילום, חדרי ישיבות, קפסולות לקפה ללא תוספת תשלום, קו טלפון כולל אלף דקות שיחה לכל משרד, ייעוץ עסקי שכלול במחיר, בכל חודש יש מפגש נטוורקינג לכל הדיירים. המשימה שלי היא לעזור לבעלי עסקים וזה יקרה בקרוב מאוד, המבנה נמצא בתהליכי בנייה מתקדמים וכבר בחודש מאי הקרוב הוא יתחיל לעבוד". "כולם מסייעים לכולם" אלעד מכוון לכל בעלי העסקים, למתחילים ולאלו שכבר נמצאים שנים רבות בשוק, "כולם מגיעים אלינו, יש חברות קטנות וחדשות לצד חברות גדולות וכולם מסייעים לכולם, זה כל הרעיון, זה מעין קהילה מתקדמת שתסייע לכל נותני השירות בקניון לקבל לקוחות, העלות החודשית הנמוכה שווה פרסום בסכום זהה בכל פלטפורמה אחרת, אנחנו פשוט עוזרים להם לקבל לקוחות חדשים. האם הקניון המסורתי כפי שאנחנו מכירים אותו היום ייעלם בקרוב? לאלעד יש תשובה מעניינת מאוד, "היום כולם באינטרנט, הקניונים הרגילים עומדים למות. כשרוצים שירות מבעל עסק יושבים מולו ולא מדברים אתו באינטרנט. הכול משתנה ונותני השירות יהיו הקניונים החדשים, בגדים ואופנה עוברים לאינטרנט, העלויות יורדות וניתן לראות את זה במגמה מאוד ברורה בשנים האחרונות, רשתות ענק עוזבות את ישראל וכבר עכשיו אנחנו במשא ומתן להכניס SUCCESS CENTER גם לקניונים רגילים, הקניון העסקי הראשון שייפתח במאי יהיה הראשון, זה יקרה בתל אביב והאופק נראה מעניין מאוד בכל התחום הזה, צפויות הפתעות נוספות". כאיש עסקים שחצה את האוקיינוס והצליח במדינות רבות ברחבי העולם, לאלעד יש כמה טיפים לעסקן המתחיל. "הדבר החשוב ביותר הוא לדעת מאיפה אתה מביא את הלקוחות שלך, אם בן אדם שפותח עסק לא יודע בוודאות מאיפה מגיעה התנועה שלו אז זה לא שווה שום דבר. קודם כל חשוב לדעת מאיפה אתה מביא לקוחות ועבודה, אם עלויות הפרסום עולות על ההכנסות זה כבר לא שווה כלום".

# From Shopping Mall to Consumer Purchases to Business Operations

## The Digital Revolution Forcing Traditional Malls to Change

Massive online shopping is eating away at stores and pushing malls to take on new forms. One creative and original direction is transforming them into service malls for businesses.

In recent years, we are witnessing a change in consumption habits throughout the world. Malls are emptying out, some are closing, and large chains are weakening and earning much less thanks to direct online shopping. Traditional malls are being replaced by online stores that offer a very wide variety of products at much lower prices without needing to leave home. Are we approaching the disappearance of malls? If you ask Elad Dar, an entrepreneur and businessman, he would answer you very clearly—they are not going to disappear, they will simply change. Meet the Israeli businessman who is establishing the first mall that will provide comprehensive solutions for business owners and professionals.

Elad Dar (41) from Tel Aviv left school at age 16 and a half, to his parents' dismay. In conversation with him, he tells of the big dreams he had since his youth. "I told them I wanted to be independent, even though they thought I was going in a completely different direction. You could say not everyone believed I would succeed. At age 20, I had a company that provided services to lawyers, with messengers throughout the country. At 23, I moved from Nesher Ziona to Tel Aviv, rented an office, and almost went bankrupt. I immediately realized I had no idea how to run a business despite all my big dreams. I understood that I had to consult with experts and learn properly how to manage my life's enterprise. So I decided to get business consulting, and within five months my business grew six times over. Right after the success, I decided I also wanted to study business consulting. At that time, I opened another company and both companies ran on their own, money flowed, and I became specialized."

## "I Promised I Would Stay in Israel"

Dar's success continued and within just five years he turned the school where he studied into an international success. "After I finished my studies in 2006, I decided to open a business consulting company called SUCCESS. In 2009, I had a shortage of manpower and simply bought the college where I studied business consulting, Herbert College. Thanks to the tools I acquired in my studies, I managed to leverage my acquisition, and in 2011 I started lecturing around the world on methods I had developed. A year later, I opened the first college branch in the Czech Republic, and within three years, 15 branches opened in many countries around the world, including Holland, Germany, and the United States."

Beyond being a successful businessman, he had a dream. Elad was a father to four sons and always dreamed of a daughter. His wife, who had dealt with raising children while he spent considerable time abroad on business, made bringing another child conditional on his staying in Israel to work. Elad agreed, and so it was.

"At that time, something else happened—I had four sons born to me," he says. "My wife told me it was hard for her that I was always abroad and she had to raise the children alone. The big difficulty came when I asked for another child. I really wanted a daughter, so I promised her I would stay in Israel, and so it was. My wife became pregnant and our little daughter Nia was born to us. So after I consulted for many people and helped them make their businesses succeed, it was time for me to invest in myself.

"Now, after choosing to stay and work in Israel, I decided to establish the first business mall in the world. I thought about it about ten years ago but didn't have the money to make the idea happen. Now it's happening and in a big way."

## What Exactly Is a Business Mall?

"It's a unique model like no other—a building where professionals provide services to businesses. The mall is limited to two professionals in each field. The idea is to provide business owners and professionals in Israel with a range of all service providers. There are rooms called 'New York' and 'Wall Street.'"

"Every month there is a networking meeting for all the tenants."

"It's a mall where every client who enters it is a client of all the shop owners in the mall. For example, a business owner needs the services of a lawyer, graphic designer, content writer, accountant, and other services. Here I bring them all together into one large, sophisticated business mall. The building is equipped with the most advanced technology so that anyone in the building will get work just by being in the building. The mall itself will provide all the services to business owners."

## "A Lot of Courage and Faith"

Elad's vision is that clients of one of the building's clients will become clients of all the others. There are two professionals from each field so the client can compare work quality and prices, and thus can get solutions for all their needs in one place.

"The client must have a choice option, and therefore I chose to allow more than one professional from each field to work in the business mall," he explains. "Beyond the fact that everyone is in the same compound, the entire building is equipped with a smart television system that allows every guest in the building to be exposed to other service providers in the building. How do you convert an office building into an apartment? On one hand, there is a severe shortage of residential apartments. On the other hand, many office buildings stand empty. The solution sounds simple, so why is it so complicated? The proposal in the Knesset hasn't passed yet, but developers are already beginning to plan office-to-residential conversions. More and more developers are seeking to examine how to change zoning partially or fully in projects located in employment zones or areas designated for mixed-use. The absurdity: developers will profit from zoning changes to residential, but local authority heads will lose from the public coffers. The Arrangements Law stipulates that up to 50% of built office space can be converted to residential and up to 30% of building rights for offices in unrealized projects can be converted to small residential apartments. Tito Architects' office, for example, is currently planning a project originally designated for offices only, and now designers are planning a mixed-use complex of offices and residential equally. The residential units will be on the upper floors, small apartments with an average area of about 50 square meters.

The Finance Ministry addressed giant commercial and employment complexes being built in Israel and existing ones, and sought to convert up to 50% of office buildings to residential apartments. The only problem: opposition from local authority heads, without whom the plan cannot be implemented. The reason for opposition: the property tax rate for commerce and offices is much higher than for residential. Harm alongside benefit

In Britain, the government extended the permit for developers to convert office buildings to residential without the need to comply with building and planning regulations for residential. The British Guardian reported on converting offices to small apartments of 16 square meters, without windows and without minimum living conditions. This situation contradicts our fair rental law, which passed with great difficulty in Israel. The current reality is a celebration for contractors. The Contractors Association is implementing a plan to reduce apartment rents and prices by renovating and converting thousands of offices to residential. The association claims that there are tens of thousands of offices in demand areas that can be converted with renovations of just a month to a residence. Such a move could add tens of thousands of apartments and thus reduce apartment rents and housing prices. Eran Siv, chairman of the Contractors Association: "It is possible and can add tens of thousands of housing units in a very short time. I am confident that this program will significantly reduce rents for young couples and students, and could add tens of thousands more quality housing units."

A bypass route around bureaucracy

According to Peigelan, a critical condition for the law's existence is a process as simple as possible, without dependence on additional planning procedures or exemptions. "We must anchor the developer's right to submit a building permit request to convert office rights to 50% residential without any additional procedure," he emphasizes. Israel is short about 190,000 apartments, and as demographic growth continues the shortage will worsen."

In one building, retail, offices, residential, hotels, culture, leisure and entertainment are combined. When you build a tower of 120 to 160 floors costing about 2 billion dollars, you can't risk occupancy decline. Implementing options for every needed use allows the tower to breathe. If in a certain year there's more need for residential, you add floors at the expense of offices. If you need more hotels, you add floors at the expense of residential. In summary, it is an evil idea, a non-original extraction that sounds every few years, usually during the change of relevant ministers. Above all, it is anti-planning and an idea that local authorities will not support, and therefore it will not be promoted in practice, mainly due to property tax considerations, but not only." Architect Yoav Oman, owner and partner of Tito-Oman Architects, believes that this is an excellent move. "In the corona year, there was a significant change in work patterns, and many moved to work from home. Some companies are adopting a hybrid work model, and estimates are that the new situation will create large surpluses of employment space in the office market, which some would say was already saturated even before the corona. In Israel, there are about 190,000 apartments lacking, and as the demographic growth continues, the shortage will worsen." Dalia Assis, a real estate appraiser, city planner and lecturer in real estate at Bar-Ilan University: "The critical shortage of residential apartments in the demand area and the significant surplus of employment space, offices and commerce, necessitate this decision. The dichotomy that has developed over the years between residential areas and employment areas is problematic for two reasons: the long commute makes it difficult for workers and causes great waste to the economy, and employment areas become desolate in the evening." She notes that in order for the process to succeed, it must be promoted with maximum coordination with local authorities. "The needs for housing must be examined in each place, and not to produce a schematic model of one-third residential and two-thirds employment, which is not necessarily good for every place." Architect Gil Shani, Chairman of CTBUH - International Council on Tall Buildings in Israel: "For many years, the world has recognized mixed uses. In one building, we combine commerce, employment, residential, hospitality, culture, recreation and leisure. When building a tower of 120 to 160 floors at about 2 billion dollars, it is impossible to risk a drop in occupancy. Implementing the possibilities for each use allows the tower to breathe. If in a particular year there is a need for more residential, add floors at the expense of offices. If more hospitality is needed, add floors at the expense of residential. In the corona, we learned to function under extreme uncertainty. Whoever will survive is not the strongest, but the most flexible. We need buildings that will provide an adequate response to changing needs."

premise_he: מדינת הלכה או הלכה המדינה?  מדוע נקרא תחום המצוות והחוקים הדתיים הלכה? • מה פירוש השמות במגילת רות? • ומה התירוץ של מאיר אריאל?  הצירוף "מדינת הלכה" חזר השבוע לשיח הציבורי, בעקבות דבריו של בצלאל סמוטריץ'. מעבר לדיון האידיאולוגי, עומדת גם שאלה לשונית מעניינת: מדוע נקרא התחום הרחב של מצוות וחוקים דתיים "הלכה"? מה הקשר בין פועל התנועה "ללכת" לבין חוקים ומצוות?  התשובה מובילה לאחד המאפיינים הבולטים של השפה העברית: הפיגורטיביות, העברה של מונחים, מילים וביטויים מהתחום הפיזי לתחום המופשט. במקרה זה, פועל התנועה ללכת ומילים בשורש הל"ך עוברות מהתחום הפיזי לתחום הדיבור, המחשבה והאמונה.  "הלכה" היא מילה תלמודית נפוצה מאוד. במסכת אבות נכתב: "הלומד מחברו פרק אחד או הלכה אחת או פסוק אחד או דיבור אחד, אפילו אות אחת, צריך לנהוג בו כבוד".  המשנה והתלמוד מלאים "הלכות" בדרגות שונות של חומרה, אבל את המקור לכך אפשר למצוא כבר בתנ"ך. פעלים מן השורש הל"ך יש רבים מאוד, למעלה מ-1,500, ורובם קשורים בתנועה - אבל בכמה מהם מדובר בקיום מצוות. כמה דוגמאות, שלכל אחת מהן גרסאות נוספות:  "ואת חוקותי תשמרו ללכת בהם" (ויקרא י"ח, 4)  "ללכת בדרכיו ולשמור מצוותיו" (דברים ל', 16)  "בחוקות החיים הלך" (יחזקאל ל"ג, 15)  "באורח צדקה אֲהַלֵּך" (משלי ח', 20)  "הדרך אשר הוליכך ה' אלוהיך" (דברים ח', 2)  הרעיון פשוט: קיום מצוות הוא הליכה בדרך שהותוותה על ידי סמכות כלשהי, ועם זאת יש בה מידה של דינמיות וגמישות. לצד זה משמשת בספר איוב המילה "הליך" במשמעות רגל. בעברית החדשה זכתה המילה למשמעות חדשה: הליכים משפטיים, הליכי גירושין. המילה "הליכות" פירושה דרך התנהגות, במסגרת הצירוף "נימוסים והליכות", וזה כבר מהתנ"ך: "צופיה הליכות ביתה" (משלי ל"א, 27) וכן "הליכות עולם לו" (חבקוק ג', 6).  גם פעלי תנועה אחרים מספרים אותו סיפור. "לנהוג" הוא בתנ"ך, כמו גם היום, פועל תנועה שממנו נולדו במקורות מילים כמו "נוהג" ו"מנהג", והפועל להתנהג. "להתנהל" פירושו להתקדם בהליכה, ומכאן ניהול וגם "נוהל" בעברת החדשה. ואילו מן הרגל האנושית נולדו המילים הרגל, רגיל, להתרגל ותרגיל. כולן קשורות להתנהגות ולא להליכה פיזית.  כאן גם נעוץ ההבדל בין "הלכה" לבין "מצווה" או "חוק". מצווה היא הלכה קפואה, היא מדגישה את ההיררכיה ולא את המעשה הדינמי. חוק הוא מה שחקוק באבן, משהו שאין לשנותו. "מדינת הלכה" היא איפה אוקסימורון לשוני. "מדינה" היא מוסד או ממשל שביכולתו לקבוע דין ומשפט. "הלכה" היא מערכת דינמית, מרובת מחלוקות ומאבקים בין "פוסקי הלכות". היא מסורה לרבנים במסגרת הקהילות הדתיות, ושם עליה להישאר.  ערפה, שהפנתה עורף לחמותה  לכבוד חג השבועות מביא אורי הייטנר היבט מעניין המתייחס למגילת רות: "הדבר הקופץ מיד לעין הוא שמותיהם של גיבורי הטקסט, שממש מזמינים מדרש שמות.  אלימלך. "שהיה אומר: אליי תבוא מלכות" (מדרש רות רבה). רמז מטרים למידע על המשך השושלת, שיימסר בסוף המגילה – דוד הוא צאצא המשפחה.  נעמי. "שהיו מעשיה נאים ונעימים" (מדרש רות רבה).  מאיר אריאל ז"ל // צילום: קוקו  ח"כ בצלאל סמוטריץ' // צילום: אורן בן חקון  מחלון וכיליון. "מחלון - שנימח מן העולם וכיליון - שכלה מן העולם" (מדרש רות רבה). ואפשר לדרוש את השם מחלון, כאדם שימות ממחלה. יש להוסיף לכך מדרש מהתלמוד בבלי, מסכת בבא בתרא: "ולמה נקרא שמן מחלון וכליון? מחלון - שעשו גופן חולין, וכליון - שנתחייבו כליה למקום".  ערפה ורות. "ערפה, שהפכה עורף לחמותה... רות, שראתה בדברי חמותה".  רות. "אמר ר' יוחנן: למה נקרא שמה רות? שזכתה ויצא ממנה דוד, שריווהו להקדוש ברוך הוא בשירות ותשבחות" (ילקוט שמעוני, רות). מִדְרָשֵׁם נוסף – רות = רעות.  מבסוטיות הווירצ'ואל, שרמוטיות הויז'ואל  בחודש יולי נציין 20 שנה למותו המוקדם כל כך של מאיר אריאל. לקראת האירוע הוציאה משפחתו ספר ובו טקסטים שכתב אריאל לאורך השנים, בעריכת עטרה אופק. שם הספר, כשם אחד משיריו של אריאל: ד"ר התחכמות (הוא באמת ידע למות...). לכבוד צאת הספר נערך בשבוע שעבר ערב מיוחד בבית היוצר.  הטקסטים של אריאל משלימים את הרבגוניות של האיש המיוחד, החכם הזה ורב הקסם. בעיני, כפי שמוצג באתר הזירה הלשונית, מאיר אריאל הוא גיבור שפה, ובתחום השפה במוזיקה הישראלית הוא הגדול מכולם. בספר סוגות רבות: מכתבים, הספדים, סיפורים, הבלחות צחוק ועוד. בכמה מהם, איך לא, מתייחס אריאל אל השפה עצמה ובאחרות מלהטט בה. ולהלן דוגמיות.  מהי השפה הישראלית. "אחלה קוקטייל פארטי, וואחאד ביזנס, אוואנטה קומוניקטיבית, דאווין אסרטיבי, חליק ז'נטיליות, היפר אקטיבית, חפיף סוּפֶּר, סלבריטאות חנטרישית, סמול טוק עלק, בולשיט יעני, אינטלקטואלי עלא כיפק, סבבה און-ליין, אכבר ריבאונדר, איניות סחבקיסטית, אאוטיות בארֶדית, חארטה פוסטמודרנית, מבסוטיות הווירצ'ואל, שרמוטיות הויז'ואל, אהלן – היי, יאללה – ביי" (מתוך הספר "הישראלים" מאת מיכה קירשנר, 1997).  חזונו של מאיר. "הנה ימים באים ואנשים יאבדו את הטעם שבבריחה, ומסכות תוסרנה ותהיה הודאה על האמת. אמונות ודעות והשקפות תושלכנה ואנשים יודו בטעויות ויאמצו אמונות חדשות, פתוחות למשא ומתן. כל הממסדים והמנגנונים הידועים יתפרקו וייעלמו, וסדרי ממשל משוכללים פתוחים למשא ומתן יקומו תחתיהם. הנה ימים באים". (שנות התשעים).  תירוצים רצוצים רצונות וריצות. "ספר התירוצים הוא ספר השורש רצ"ה ותר"ץ, שמוליד רצון וריצוי לִרְצות ולְרַצות, שמולידים תירוצים בבית, בבית המשפט, בבית המדרש ובכל מיקום ועניין שיש לפה לסבר אוזן, לתרץ תירוץ, שהאוזן תרצה ותתרצה... אין ספר התירוצים מתעסק בשורשים ר"ץ ורצ"ץ, שצלצולם דומה בהטיות שונות וקרוב לשורש התירוצים והרצונות. רצתי לרצותך בתירוצים רצוצים. זה ספר הרצאת תירוצים מתורצים לרצון המתבונן למצוא חן בעיני המעיין, שיהיו הכל רוצים ונרצים". (ספר התירוצים, 1998).  על מכבסת המילים. "אני מברך על הקטע שנקרא 'מכבסת מילים', שבו מצאתי שותף לחרדה שאני עצמי נתקף לפרקים לנוכח הנדידה של מילים ממשמעותן למשמעות שונה, אם כי לא בחריפות של הדוגמאות שהבאת, אך באותה מידת סכנה. למשל, 'הלביא פורש כנפיים', 'הלביא המריא', ויש 'כפיר' ו'שחל', ואתה לא בטוח אם יישאר אריה לרפואה למלוך על החיות". (מכתב לדוד גרוסמן בעקבות "הזמן הצהוב", 1987).  על תרבות השיחה בקיבוץ. "כידוע, כל נאום באסיפה הכללית פותחים במילה: חברים! ולפני שהנואם שואף אוויר בשביל המשפט השני של נאומו, מזדרזים החברים להראות לו כמה הם חברים באמת: מתפרצים, משסעים, תוקעים דברים שלא לעניין. דבר שגורר את כולם למערבולת שהכל בה, חוץ ממה שצריך להיות באמת". (דרשה באסיפת קיבוץ משמרות, שנות השמונים).  על נעמי שמר. "נעמי שמר – בשביל שמרמורת נועם... נעמי זמר – בשביל זמרמורת נעימות חסידיות... נעמי צמר – בשביל צמרמורת נעימה... נעמי גֶמֶר – בשביל גמרמורת בנעימים". (עם זכייתה של נעמי שמר בפרס ישראל, 1983).  על נתן אלתרמן. "בשביל כוכבים בחיתולים. סנאי על כתפי היער. חלב הפונדקית. סופי הדרכים המה רק געגוע. באש נושק הפה אשר נקרע לקרוא לאדמה הזאת מולדת. איזה זרם חיובי-שלילי רץ-מקפץ כעל גחלים: באש (שלילי), נושק (חיובי) הפה (חיובי) אשר נקרע (שלילי) לקרוא (חיובי) לאדמה (חיובי) הזאת (שלילי) מולדת (חיובי). ... צלקת אלתרמן – צליל, משקל, קצב, ניגון, ברק, מחשבה – לא עזבה אותי שנים".
