# A State of Halakha or Halakha of the State?

Why is the domain of commandments and religious laws called "halakha"? What is the meaning of the names in the Book of Ruth? And what is Meir Ariel's solution?

The term "halakha state" returned to public discourse this week, following statements by Bezalel Smotrich. Beyond the ideological debate, there is also an interesting linguistic question: why is the broad domain of commandments and religious laws called "halakha"? What is the connection between the verb of movement "to go" and laws and commandments?

The answer leads to one of the prominent characteristics of the Hebrew language: figurativeness—the transfer of terms, words, and expressions from the physical domain to the abstract domain. In this case, the verb of movement "to go" and words from the root h-l-k undergo a transition from the physical domain to the domain of speech, thought, and belief.

"Halakha" is a very common Talmudic word. In Pirkei Avot it is written: "One who learns from his fellow one chapter, or one halakha, or one verse, or one saying, or even one letter, should treat him with honor."

The Mishnah and Talmud are full of "halakhot" in varying degrees of severity, but the source for this can already be found in the Bible. There are very many verbs from the root h-l-k—over 1,500—and most are related to movement, but some of them deal with the fulfillment of commandments. A few examples, each with additional versions:

"And you shall keep My statutes to walk in them" (Leviticus 18:4)

"To walk in His ways and to keep His commandments" (Deuteronomy 30:16)

"He walked in the statutes of life" (Ezekiel 33:15)

"In the path of righteousness I walk" (Proverbs 8:20)

"The way that the Lord your God has led you" (Deuteronomy 8:2)

The idea is simple: fulfilling commandments is walking in a path that has been marked out by some authority, and yet there is within it a measure of dynamism and flexibility. Alongside this, the word "halikh" (gait) is used in the Book of Job to mean leg. In modern Hebrew, the word acquired a new meaning: legal proceedings, divorce proceedings. The word "halikhot" means manner of behavior, in the phrase "customs and manners," which already appears in the Bible: "She watches over the ways of her household" (Proverbs 31:27) and "The everlasting ways are His" (Habakkuk 3:6).

Other verbs of movement tell the same story. "To conduct" is in the Bible, as it is today, a verb of movement from which words such as "custom" and "manner" were born in the sources, along with the verb "to behave." "To proceed" means to advance by walking, and from this come management and also "manual" in modern Hebrew. And from the human leg came the words "habit," "accustomed," "to accustom," and "exercise." They are all related to behavior and not to physical movement.

Here lies the difference between "halakha" and "commandment" or "law." A commandment is halakha frozen in place; it emphasizes hierarchy rather than dynamic action. Law is what is engraved in stone, something that cannot be changed. "A halakha state" is somewhat of a linguistic oxymoron. A "state" is an institution or government capable of establishing judgment and law. "Halakha" is a dynamic system, rich with disputes and struggles among "halakha decisors." It is entrusted to rabbis within the framework of religious communities, and there it should remain.

# Orpah, Who Turned Her Back on Her Mother-in-Law

In honor of the holiday of Shavuot, Uri Heitner presents an interesting perspective related to the Book of Ruth: "What immediately catches the eye is the names of the heroes of the text, which practically invite midrashic interpretation:

Elimelech: "He was saying: 'To me shall kingship come'" (Midrash Ruth Rabbah). A hint in the metrics about information regarding the continuation of the dynasty, which will be transmitted at the end of the scroll—David is a descendant of the family.

Naomi: "Her deeds were pleasant and pleasing" (Midrash Ruth Rabbah).

Mahlon and Chilion: "Mahlon—because he was smitten from the world; Chilion—because he perished from the world" (Midrash Ruth Rabbah). One can also interpret the name Mahlon as a person who dies from illness. To this we should add a midrash from the Talmud Bavli, in Tractate Bava Batra: "And why were they called Mahlon and Chilion? Mahlon—because they made their bodies unhealthy; Chilion—because they were punished with destruction before the Almighty."

Orpah and Ruth: "Orpah, who turned her back on her mother-in-law... Ruth, who heeded her mother-in-law's words."

Ruth: "Rabbi Yochanan said: Why was she called Ruth? Because she merited and David came from her, whom the Holy One, blessed be He, rewarded with songs and praises" (Yalkut Shimoni, Ruth). Another midrash—Ruth = companions.

# From Virtual Cheerfulness to Visual Mischief

In July we will mark 20 years since the untimely death of Meir Ariel. In preparation for the event, his family published a book containing texts Ariel wrote over the years, edited by Atura Opak. The name of the book, like one of Ariel's songs: "The Doctor of Cleverness (He Really Knew How to Die...)." To mark the book's publication, a special evening was held last week at the artist's studio.

Ariel's texts complement the versatility of this special man, this wise and charming rabbi. In my view, as presented on the Linguistic Arena website, Meir Ariel is a language hero, and in the realm of language in Israeli music he is the greatest of all. The book contains many genres: letters, eulogies, stories, humorous sketches, and more. In some of them, Ariel naturally addresses language itself, and in others he plays with it. Here are some examples.

What is Israeli language: "The coolest cocktail party, and one business, avant communicative, and then assertive, smooth gentility, hyper-active, overlapping super, celebrity snobbish, small talk slick, bullshit basically, intellectual-schmintellectual, fine online, a comeback bouncer, innate scheming, outish vulgarity, a postmodern charter, from virtual cheerfulness, visual mischief, hello—hey, yalla—bye." (From the book "The Israelis" by Micha Kirshenblatt, 1997).

Meir's vision: "Behold, days are coming and people will lose the taste of escape, and masks will be removed and there will be confession of truth. Beliefs and opinions and outlooks will be cast away and people will confess to mistakes and adopt new beliefs, open to negotiation. All known institutions and mechanisms will disintegrate and disappear, and refined systems of government open to negotiation will be established in their place. Behold, days are coming." (1990s).

Explanations fractured by desires and runnings: "The Book of Explanations is a book of the root r-tz-h and t-r-tz, which generates will and satisfaction, to please and to satisfy, which generate explanations in the home, in the courtroom, in the study hall, and in every place and matter that there is a mouth to argue, to provide an explanation, so that the ear is pleased and satisfied... The Book of Explanations does not deal with the roots r-tz and r-tz-tz, whose sound is similar in various declensions and close to the root of explanations and desires. I wanted to please you with fractured explanations. This is a book of a presentation of explanations explained to the satisfaction of the observer to find favor in the eyes of the reader, so that all are pleased and satisfied." (Book of Explanations, 1998).

On the laundry of words: "I bless the section called 'Word Laundry,' in which I found a partner in the anxiety that sometimes grips me in the face of the wandering of words from their meaning to a different meaning, though not with the sharpness of the examples you brought, but with the same degree of danger. For example, 'the lion spreads his wings,' 'the lion took off,' and there are 'young lion' and 'jackal,' and you're not sure if a lion will remain to practice medicine to rule over the beasts." (Letter to David Grossman following "The Yellow Time," 1987).

On the culture of discourse in the kibbutz: "As is known, every speech at the general assembly begins with the word: 'Comrades!' and before the speaker takes a breath for the second sentence of his speech, the comrades hurry to show him how truly comrades they are: they burst forth, split, interject things irrelevant to the matter. A thing that drags them all into a whirlpool where everything in it, except what should really be there, exists." (Sermon at a kibbutz assembly, 1980s).

On Naomi Shemer: "Naomi Shemer—for the shivers of pleasantness... Naomi Zamer—for the shivers of Hasidic melodies... Naomi Tzmer—for pleasant shivers... Naomi Gamer—for shivers in melodies." (Upon Naomi Shemer's winning the Israel Prize, 1983).

On Nathan Alterman: "For stars in swaddling clothes. A squirrel on the shoulders of the forest. The milk of the inn. The ends of the roads are only longing. What positive-negative current runs-bounces like on embers: in fire (negative), kisses (positive), the mouth (positive) which is torn (negative) to call (positive) to the earth (positive) that (negative) homeland (positive)... Alterman's scar—sound, weight, rhythm, melody, brightness, thought—did not leave me for years." (Stations of influence and inspiration in my life, 1995).

On men of action, poor in spirit: "So stop already talking all the time in the tone of five-six-ton-apples-per-dunam, or in the tone of cubic-meter-per-hour, or in the tone of concrete. And raise your eyes a bit, which look only downward all the time, measuring only your height, yes: raise your eyes also around you—there is space... above you—there is height... maybe you'll see some hovering sparkle... some spirit man signaling... maybe you'll even be ashamed, you men of action." (Main title, 1986).

# The Child Who Lived in a Balagan

Several responses came following the discussion of the multilingual word "balagan." Rafi Ashet writes: "Balagan means tent in Russian. I told an old friend (93) and he remembered, that 48 years ago they were in tents, and a Russian mother came to visit her son and said to him: 'Oh, you live in a balagan.'"

Esther Samueli writes: "To the balakhan-balkhan-balagan one can add the Balkan mountains and countries, whose etymology according to researchers is identical to that of the former." It turns out this is indeed so. Researchers are divided on the origin of the name Balkan, which means in Turkish 'chain of wooded mountains.' Similar words are found in various Turkish languages, but the origin leads to Persian. Some believe the origin is in 'balak-mod' which means swampy forest. Another opinion is that the origin of Balkan is indeed in bala-khana in Persian, which means high and large house, and it is also the origin of balagan.

# I Traveled to Harmi'el with a Nun and Clay

Sigal writes: "I wish to consult, or more precisely to deliberate, regarding the proper vocalization of certain words in standard form. In your opinion, is there room in certain texts to make exceptions to the rule, and this for reasons of preserving sound? For example, to vocalize the verb 'to pickpocket' as such, instead of the standard form 'to pickpocket.'

For the non-standard form sounds much more natural and friendly, and despite its lack of standardness, it does not sound too harsh as does the standard form, or when the linguistic-social situation in the book requires non-standard pronunciation. I would be happy to hear your opinion."

The issue is much broader than certain verbs. The laws of begad-kefet are implemented in a very partial way in spoken language. Netiva Ben-Yehuda defined the phenomenon when she scolded Dalia Mazor who spoke about "a film about a nun and clay," when of course she meant a nun and a priest.

No resident of the Galilean city would say he is "traveling to Harmi'el," and another would go to Petach Tikva not to Petah Tikva, and certainly not to Poland. Nevertheless, in many cases the rules are preserved even in spoken language. To spoil and not to spoil, to cook and not to cook, and so on. In the realm of the verb, it appears the main problems are with verbs beginning with the consonant k.

And regarding the question, the issue naturally arises only in vocalized texts, and these are generally aimed at books of poetry and children's books. In these, despite sometimes being foreign, it is important to maintain normative vocalization, and deviate from it only when dealing with spoken dialogue. Most texts are not vocalized and the problem does not exist. On the other hand, in free speech excessive adherence to the rules creates foreignness, and it is better to preserve it for cases where precise pronunciation is required.

# Italian, Kosher and Delicious: Chianti According to Halacha

Terra di Seta winery, located in the heart of Chianti region in Italy, is a kosher winery despite not being obligated to be one, and it offers a wonderful experience, excellent wines and even a kosher dairy restaurant • Our correspondent visited there and returned with a treasure trove of experiences and recommendations

It wasn't difficult to miss the narrow gravel path leading to the boutique Tuscan winery "Terra di Seta," nestled in the heart of Chianti region. The paved road that took us from the city of Siena had ended several kilometers earlier, but Waze led us onto an unpaved road within the dark forest. Only by luck did we spot the modest sign Agriturismo Terra di Seta - pointing to an even narrower path. Upon arrival, we were warmly greeted by Daniel della Seta, the property owner, whose complex includes, beyond the winery building, his private residence, three stunning and secluded guest accommodations, a swimming pool overlooking the horizon, a kosher dairy restaurant (open during tourist season), a vegetable garden where all vegetables and greens for the menu are grown, natural forest, and of course - more than 150 acres of vineyard (almost entirely Sangiovese) and olive groves. The view from every direction opens the heart - rows upon rows of vineyards in varying shades of green, and cypress trees with upright trunks stretching skyward. Every encounter we have with Tuscany is moving, especially one where you discover a wonderful and kosher winery.

The della Seta family is of deep Roman Jewish roots, and their name hints at their historical occupation - weaving of prayer shawls from silk, which were once common among Rome's Jews. Daniel is a biologist by training and served as a lecturer in the field at the Italian Academy. He came to winemaking and agriculture following his wife. "We decided to purchase the property at the beginning of the millennium and in the first years we sold the grapes to wineries in the area," he tells us while strolling through the vineyards at sunset. "In 2007 we understood that we wanted to make our own wine, we built the new winery, and from the start we made the decision to voluntarily subject ourselves to three regulatory systems - that of the Chianti Classico region, organic regulation and the kosher law system. Since the vineyards were old and tired, we started replanting (uprooting the old vines and replanting the vineyards anew) the entire area, plot by plot, and only in the next harvest, 2022, will we harvest grapes from the last replanted plot."

Which regulatory system is the most challenging? Della Seta: "I'm not sure there's an answer to that question. In every regulatory system there are more complex and less complex aspects, and some even overlap. For example, according to both Jewish halacha and the laws of Chianti Classico, the oldest wine region in Italy, in the first three years of vine planting the fruit cannot be used. The soil here is rocky and difficult to work, so the planting process was complex and expensive, but for that reason it's also good for vines, and their roots struggle to penetrate deep into it and reach the water located beneath the surface even without irrigation, which is forbidden here in Chianti. The winery wall, by the way, we built from the stones we cleared from our vineyards."

For wine production, he enlisted renowned Italian wine consultant Enrico Paternoster, who among other things is responsible for the important wine research institute in the land of apple wine, located in Trentino - Istituto Agrario di San Michele all'Adige (IASMA). Paternoster excels at expressing the regional nuances of Chianti in his wines.

The restaurant kitchen produces only local and seasonal dishes based on local agricultural products. Don't look for rare raw materials or pretentious dishes there - everything is based on traditional rural Tuscan cuisine, but what cuisine! Among other things, a wonderful "pappa al pomodoro" is served there - a thick tomato soup made of tomatoes, bread, olive oil, garlic and basil, various bruschettas, panzanella salad, fresh pasta, local fish and more, alongside the winery's wines of course. So simple - so precise and delicious.

Four out of the five winery wines, by the way, are also available in Israel, so whether you've already started planning your upcoming Italian vacation, or if you're staying in the country for now - you can already start enjoying them here.

**Vino di Seta Rosato, 2020** - The only rosé from the winery, yet it too is made 100% from Sangiovese grapes that did not undergo pressing. Its color, contrary to the fashion decree ruling in Israel, shines and sparkles, with a floral and charming nose, a good body of young red fruit and emphasized minerality in a silky texture with a long finish. A delightful wine (12 euros, available at the winery only).

**Toscana, 2019** - The winery's red entry wine, with almost no wood contact (only two months in previously-used barrels), also made 100% Sangiovese. Ahmad Tibi (Raam-Taal): Any reasonable person who is asked...

Avraham Dikter (Minister of Internal Security): I agree that considering the alternative, I would listen to Minister Ruhma. Anyway, regarding warnings to Arab leaders...

Come with Me to the Festival

On Thursday the Haifa Film Festival will open • A house correspondent recommends a few films to be screened there

The 30th edition of the Haifa Film Festival, opening this coming Thursday with a screening of "The Judge," starring Robert Downey Jr. and Robert Duvall, offers this year a long and almost exaggerated array of fascinating and recommended films.

Want more updates? Join Israel Today on Facebook

Besides an intriguing Israeli competition featuring, among others, "A Good Death" by Sharon Maymon and Tal Granit, "Jonah" by Nir Bergman, "You to Me at Night" by Assaf Korman, and "Manpower" by Noam Kaplan, and besides a visit by the excellent Russian director Andrei Zvyagintsev ("The Return," "The Banishment"), who will present his acclaimed new film "Leviathan," the festival will also screen some of the most talked-about works of the past year, such as "Winter Sleep" by Nuri Bilge Ceylan ("Once Upon a Time in Anatolia"), which won the Palme d'Or at the recent Cannes Festival, and the American "Whiplash," which won the grand prize at the Sundance Festival.

To make it easier for you to navigate the rich program, here are a few more films, somewhat less known, that are definitely worth being aware of.

• "20,000 Days on Earth": Singer-poet-writer-screenwriter Nick Cave has disappeared somewhat in recent years, but this thrilling, stylish and inspiring musical biography, which stands somewhere between an artistic documentary and a self-portrait, is sure to delight and move anyone who has been captivated by his unique charm over the years. Directors Ian Forsyth and Jane Pollard take Cave on a journey to the past, send him to sift through archive photos, introduce him to prominent figures he collaborated with (such as Björk Guðmundsdóttir and Kylie Minogue) and accompany him as he works on his new album. Cave, who turned 57 this year, opens up to the camera, reveals fascinating details about his creative process, philosophizes as if there were no tomorrow, and of course, also sings. A huge film about a huge artist.

• "Ida": After several decades of working in England, Polish director Paweł Pawlikowski returns to his homeland to present a stunning black-and-white drama set in the early 1960s. At the center of the plot stands a young and innocent nun who sets out with her Jewish (and communist) aunt on a roots journey in search of her family who were murdered during the Nazi occupation. Through stunning monochromatic cinematography and superb performances by the two women, Pawlikowski creates a tight and precise film containing enormous amounts of sorrow and guilt. "Ida" arrives in Haifa after garnering praise at countless festivals and after being earmarked as a leading candidate for winning the Best Foreign Film Oscar at the upcoming ceremony. In its case, the hype is completely justified.

• "Like Cattle": British director David Mackenzie ("Spread," "Perfect Sense") may not be particularly consistent, but his new film is undoubtedly one of his best. It's a visceral, violent and unexpected prison drama that follows Eric (Jake O'Connell), an angry young prisoner who is placed in a detention facility meant for adult inmates. The fact that his father (Ben Mendelsohn), whom he hasn't seen since he was five, is also imprisoned there, is supposed to help him survive, but in reality only makes things more complicated and dangerous. O'Connell (expected to become a star following his appearance here) and Mendelsohn ("Killing Them Softly") simply set the screen on fire, and Mackenzie manages to make the charged relationship that develops between them complex, extraordinary and unforgettable.

• "Clouds of Sils Maria": French director Olivier Assayas ("Irma Vep," "Summer Hours," "Carlos") is also not known for consistency, but as in Mackenzie's case, he too is at peak form in his new film. Juliette Binoche plays an aging film star, Kristen Stewart plays her personal assistant, and Assayas uses both of them to delicately and mockingly probe the creative process, performance, aging and female jealousy. Binoche delivers one of her best performances in recent years. The excellent Stewart proves there is life after "Twilight," and Chloë Grace Moretz ("Kick-Ass"), who appears in a guest role, also manages to leave her mark. The result is elegant, enigmatic and thought-provoking, and if you wish, you can see it as the feminine version of "Molière on a Bicycle."

• "Killer Joe": Michael C. Hall ("Dexter"), Sam Shepard and Don Johnson star in a dark and trashy Texas thriller from horror director Jim Mickle (responsible for the American remake of the Mexican cannibal film "We Are What We Are"). A law-abiding family man kills a burglar who broke into his home and finds himself swept into a violent and chilling maelstrom involving corrupt cops, gangsters and snuff films. On paper you've already seen this film before, but Mickle and his regular screenwriter Nick Damici navigate the work in surprising directions. The three leads gleefully commit themselves to the apparently inferior material, and genre fans are sure to leave the theater with a sickly smile.

• "Corn Island": The big winner at the Karlovy Vary Festival is a film festival par excellence. It takes place entirely on a small island in the Mtkvari River that separates Georgia from Abkhazia, has almost no dialogue, and most of its minutes are devoted to methodically following an old man and his granddaughter engaged in agricultural work. Yet if you fancy diving into a fascinating and very special cinematic experience, and you are blessed with a bit more patience than average, "Corn Island" by Giorgi Ovsiannikov, which tells a simple parable about man, nature and eternal political conflicts, is undoubtedly the film for you.

• "Truffaut Forever": Alongside some of the greatest works of legendary French director François Truffaut ("Two English Girls," "Jules and Jim" and "The 400 Blows"), to be screened at the festival marking 30 years since his death, this new documentary, directed by Alexandre Moua, will also be screened. You won't find earth-shattering revelations here, but through old interviews with the great director, perusal of his personal letters and conversations with his friends and colleagues, Moua's delicate, modest and not very long work sketches a moving human portrait of a great filmmaker and awakens a strong desire to watch again the splendid body of his work.

"מצאתי אותו בטיקטוק כשחיפשתי דואטים בעברית. למדתי את השיר כדי להרשים את הארוס שלי, אבל הוא אמר לי שהמבטא שלי לא טוב, אז שמעתי אותו שוב ושוב. מוזס הסביר לי מה פירוש המילים כדי שאני אבין מה שאני אומרת". יוצא לך לשמוע מוזיקה ישראלית בכללי? "יצא לי לשמוע שירים ישנים יותר, למשל דנה אינטרנשיונל מהאירוויזיון. אני אוהבת את המוזיקה שלה אבל זה סגנון ישן קצת. אני גם מאוד אוהבת את נטע ברזילי. אני מתה על התרבות הישראלית, את היהדות, כל מה שקשור לזה". אור בתקופות חשוכות כאמור, אליעד לא היה היחיד להגיב על הקאבר בעברית. הסרטון בעל התפאורה והאפקטים המושקעים, שתוך מספר ימים צבר כ-150 אלף צפיות, קיבל כמעט פי שניים סימוני "אנלייק" לעומת "לייק" ותגובות רבות שנעות בין זעם לבין הטחת עלבונות. כאמור, אין זו הפעם הראשונה שסרטוניה שנויים במחלוקת. כשהיא נשאלת על הסיבות שלדעתה גרמו לצופים להגיב ברשעות כלפיה, ועל כך שנראה שהמגמה שבה סרטוניה מקבלים יותר "אנלייקים" מ"לייקים" נמשכת כבר תקופה ארוכה, היא טוענת שאינה יודעת למה, אבל מסבירה שלדעתה אנשים נתלים במי שהיתה בעבר – ולא רוצים לראות אותה משתנה. "הייתה לי המון שנאה בלב, אבל השתניתי, ואנשים לא מוכנים לקבל את זה", היא אומרת. "מבחינתי זה בסדר, אני תמיד מוצאת אור בתקופות חשוכות, ויכולה להוות עדות חיה למישהי שהשתנתה בגדול. כשהתחלתי לקבל את כל השנאה הזאת כלפיי הבנתי שאני צריכה לשנות את עצמי ולהפוך לחיובית, ועכשיו אני עושה מדיטציה, בוחרת להרגיש טוב ומרגישה טוב". "אני לא מבינה יותר מדי את הקונפליקט, אבל מאז שאני עם מוזס ואנחנו מדברים על ישראל אנשים ממש מתעצבנים מזה" אם פייטס באמת אינה יודעת מה גרם לגלי השנאה כלפיה, או שמא היא מעדיפה להצניע את הסיבות, קשה לומר, כי שערוריות היו מנת חלקה תקופה ארוכה. בין היתר היא הכריזה שהיא מזדהה כטרנסג'נדרית ומרגישה כגבר הומוסקסואל כי היא "נמשכת לגברים גאים ואוהבת גלאם וזוהר"; שאינה מזדהה עוד כבן אדם; ביקשה שישתמשו בכינוי גוף רבים כשמדברים עליה; עשתה שימוש בבלאקפייס. היא גם הכריזה שיש לה הפרעת זהות, והודתה שיש לה צורך קבוע בתשומת לב. בריאיון ל"ביזנס אינסיידר" היא חשפה שחלק מהסרטונים היותר הזויים שלה הועלו "רק כדי לקבל צפיות", וכן הודתה שהיא לפעמים מציגה את עצמה כ"מטומטמת יותר ממה שהיא באמת", כי לדבריה אנשים לא היו צופים בה אם הייתה נאמנה לעצמה ולמי שהיא. אבל יאמרו מה שיגידו עליה, ותגיד היא בעצמה מה שתרצה, יש דברים שאי אפשר לקחת לה, ובהם ההספק מעורר הפליאה שלה בנבכיי תעשיית הבידור העולמית. פייטס הוציאה 11 ספרים (ששמותיהם, בתרגום חופשי, נעים בין "ההיסטוריה של אי השפיות שלי" ל"101 שירים על האקס שלי"), סדרת מוצרי טיפוח לפנים (שהתקבלה בתגובות מעורבות) והספיקה לתעד את חייה המלאים, כולל אהבות, פרידות, סכסוכים, בינג'ים ובכי על רצפת המטבח באינספור סרטונים, כשהכל ארוז בתוך אישיות עליזה, זוהרת, מצחקקת ובעלת רצון טוב, שלא תמיד מתממש. אוהבת בחורים יהודים את מוזס, ארוסה הישראלי בן ה-44, הכירה פייטס דרך אחותו, הילה, שנשואה ליוטיובר המצליח איתן קליין, כוכב רשת בזכות עצמו שמפיק פודקאסטים שזוכים למיליוני צפיות. "השתתפתי בפודקאסט שלהם ותוך כדי כך התחיל סגר הקורונה, שבגללו האח מוזס לא יכול היה להגיע", משחזרת פייטס. "הם סיפרו לי עליו כי הם ידעו שהוא הטייפ שלי – אני אוהבת בחורים יהודים – ואז החלטנו לעשות את הסגר ביחד, הוא ואני, ותשעה חודשים אחרי שהתחלנו לצאת – התארסנו". מוזס, שנוכח ברבים מאוד מסרטוניה, נראה בדיוק ההפך הגמור מפייטס – רגוע, שקט ושליו. "הוא לא מתעצבן אף פעם וזה מה שעוזר לי להירגע", היא צוחקת. חוגגת את ראש השנה. טרישה פייטס היה לך קשר לישראל או ליהדות לפני כן? "תמיד נמשכתי לתרבות הזאת ויצאתי עם יהודים, אבל גם אם הם היו מאוד בעניין הם לא רצו להתחתן איתי כי לא הייתי יהודייה, או שלא לקחו אותי ברצינות כשאמרתי שאני מוכנה להתגייר. עם מוזס זה בכלל לא היווה עניין לדיון, הוא אמר לי שאני בכלל לא חייבת להתגייר. בעיניי יהודים הם בני זוג יותר מכבדים". את עדיין חושבת להתגייר? "תכננתי להתגייר אבל אני לא יודעת אם אספיק לפני החתונה. אנחנו רוצים להגיע לארץ בפברואר או במרץ. מוזס לא ממש דתי, אני מנסה לשמור כשרות בהרבה מקרים אבל לו זה פחות משנה. אפילו רציתי לצום ביום כיפור, והוא אמר שלא צריך ושכבר כילד הוא לא היה צם. אבל אמא שלו שומרת כשרות, ואני אוהבת את הקונספט הזה". ראיתי שהעלית כמה סרטונים שאת מקיימת בהם סדר פסח וראש השנה. "יצאתי עם יהודים אמריקנים והם לא לימדו אותי שום דבר על החגים. ראש השנה הקודם היה הראשון שלי והייתי ממש נלהבת לחגוג אותו. אנשים לא מדברים מספיק על החגים היהודיים, על מה אומרת צלחת הסדר, מבחינתי זה יותר מגניב מחג הפסחא כי זה תנכ"י". חוגגת את ליל הסדר. טרישה פייטס כשהתארסה, קיבלה לא מעט תגובות קשות בעקבות הקשר עם הבחור הישראלי. "נאלצנו לחסום הרבה תגובות בעד פלשתין ונגדנו", היא משתפת, "אנחנו לא עושים שום דבר רע, אנחנו פשוט קיימים וזה לא בא לאנשים טוב בעין. אני לא מבינה יותר מדי את הקונפליקט, אבל מאז שאני עם מוזס ואנחנו מדברים על ישראל אנשים ממש מתעצבנים מזה, מהעובדה שאת שמלת החתונה שלי מעצבת גליה להב, מזה שהוא ישראלי, שהוא שירת בצבא, אבל אני מקבלת שנאה באופן כללי, גם מיהודים שלא רוצים שאתגייר ואתחתן עם יהודי, וגם מלא-יהודים שמטיפים לי שאני עוזבת את ישו. "הייתי רוצה לעבור לישראל לפחות לשנה, אבל מוזס עוד לא סגור על זה. בכללי אין לנו תוכניות כרגע. זו פעם ראשונה שלי שאהיה בארץ, למרות שאבא שלי היה בישראל כמה פעמים כשעשה טיולים עם הכנסייה הקתולית. אני מאוד אוהבת את יפו ורוצה להתחתן שם". הצד של אליעד אליעד נחום לא הכיר את טרישה פייטס לפני כן – לא היכרות אמיתית, בכל אופן, אלא רק דרך טיקטוק. "כל שיר שהעליתי בעברית לטיקטוק זכה לדואט ממנה", הוא מספר. "היא כתבה לי שחבר שלה ישראלי וככה היא לומדת עברית. זה נחמד, אבל לא ציפיתי בכלל להפקה המטורפת של הקליפ הזה. ממש הופתעתי כשראיתי את הצילום והתחפושת המושקעת של היצור הימי בקליפ". הגיעו אליך תגובות מחו"ל? "בעיניי זה מאוד אמיץ להעלות שיר בעברית לערוץ עם מיליוני מנויים שכולם דוברי אנגלית, ועוד קליפ מושקע כל כך, שכששלחתי אותו לאנשים הם שאלו אם היא לקחה סצנות מסרט בכיכובה והדביקה על השיר. זה ריגש אותי, זה היווה עבורי מין אישור כזה, כי הרבה אומרים לי בארץ שאני שר טוב באנגלית והמוזיקה שלי יכולה לעבוד גם בחו"ל. עשיתי עכשיו דואט עם זמר אמריקני בשם רוטימי, וזו פעם ראשונה שאמן ישראלי מתארח באלבום אמריקני, לרוב זה הפוך". ראיתי תגובות שהציעו ששם השיר היה מיתרגם יותר טוב ל"your inner peace" מאשר "your silence", שנשמע כמו "השתיקה שלך". "התלבטתי בשאלה איך לקרוא לו באנגלית, אבל היה נראה לי שגם במשמעות של 'השתיקה שלך' זה מתאים. הוא נכתב בתקופת סגר הקורונה, והוא מין שיר עידוד לי ולחברה שלי. היינו תקועים בבית בחוסר מעש וכל הזמן אמרתי לה 'הכל יעבור, זו רק תקופה, אני איתך'. זה הכניס אותנו לדאון. פתאום אין הופעות, אין עבודה. מזל שהתקופה הזו חלפה".

# "I'm Dying For Israeli Culture": Interview with American YouTube Star Who Covered Elyad

Trisha Paytas is a name familiar to most Americans, and soon apparently to many Israelis too. With millions of followers on social media, controversial videos and an Israeli fiancé, she gives her first interview to Israel Today and talks about her love of Judaism, the harsh reactions she receives, and the impressive clip with a Hebrew performance of Elyad's "Your Silence"

And a surprise: which Big Brother contestant does she admire?

When you add up her followers across various social media platforms, you get a number that far exceeds Israel's population. This doesn't bother American YouTube star Trisha Paytas, who goes crazy over our local version of Big Brother. "I follow Big Brother Israel on Instagram and I'm dying over your version," says Paytas, who boasts 5.4 million followers on her YouTube channel alone ("blndsundoll4mj") and another 6.4 million followers on her TikTok channel. "I can only see short clips uploaded to YouTube from the show, but it's way more interesting than the American or British version."

Would you like to participate in the Israeli version of the reality show? "I would die for that! I'm ready to learn Hebrew 24 hours a day to participate in the show. I would also be really happy to represent Israel in Eurovision. But most importantly, I want them to know that I respect Israel and Israeli culture. Sometimes people accuse me of mocking religion when I upload videos about Judaism, and that's so not true."

Paytas, 33, knows what she's talking about. Even before she participated in season 20 of Big Brother UK in 2017, which she left after 11 days, she was already a sort of mini-celebrity and a significant internet personality who always provoked many reactions, both positive and negative. After appearances in several series, films, podcasts and various shows, launching a cover album, clips and singles—Paytas is a well-known name even to those who don't spend their time on YouTube. Those more familiar with the platform would argue whether she's a "troll" or a person with good intentions who is simply misunderstood, but the videos she uploads, in which she expresses her opinion on sensitive issues, often manage to provoke debates and considerable anger among viewers, and they are often discussed on gossip sites abroad as well.

Elyad! Oh My God

Paytas's connection to the Holy Land doesn't stop at watching Big Brother Israel in bits and pieces. Tal Moseri, Oren Hazan, and Tamir from Big Brother are just some of the Israelis she follows. Her latest explosive video, hold tight, is a cover she made of a song by Elyad Nechum called "Your Silence." She even invested in filming and editing an impressive clip together with her Israeli fiancé Moses Hackamon ("Moses"). Despite barely knowing a word of Hebrew, she performed the full version in the original language. Although it's hard to understand every word because of the thick accent, you can definitely say the result is satisfying.

Like all her videos, the cover of "Your Silence" generated many reactions, but one touched the star especially—from Elyad Nechum himself, who responded to her in English and wrote: "Good job with the song and with the Hebrew!" which made Paytas very happy, and she wrote back to him: "Elyad!! Oh my God, I love you so much!"

"I was very excited to see his response," she gushes, after a failed attempt to conduct the interview in Hebrew ("I speak small Hebrew"). "I was nervous because I didn't know how people in Israel would react to me and I didn't ask him for permission to do the cover. When I saw that he was enthusiastic, I was very happy because I really love him, he's a huge celebrity in my eyes. So I found clips from 'Sun' with Moses's help and saw everything I could get my hands on. He's amazing."

How did you even get to listen to Elyad's songs? "I found him on TikTok when I was searching for Hebrew duets. I learned the song to impress my fiancé, but he told me my accent wasn't good, so I listened to it again and again. Moses explained to me what the words mean so I could understand what I was saying."

Do you get to listen to Israeli music in general? "I got to listen to older songs, for example Dana International from Eurovision. I love her music but it's a bit of an old style. I also really love Neta Barzilai. I'm dying for Israeli culture, Judaism, everything related to it."

Light in Dark Times

As mentioned, Elyad wasn't the only one to respond to the cover in Hebrew. The video with its elaborate sets and effects, which accumulated about 150,000 views within days, received almost twice as many "dislikes" compared to "likes" and many comments ranging from anger to hurling insults. As mentioned, this is not the first time her videos are controversial. When asked about the reasons she thinks caused viewers to react maliciously toward her, and about the fact that it seems the trend of her videos receiving more dislikes than likes has been going on for a long time, she claims she doesn't know why, but explains that in her opinion people are stuck on who she used to be—and don't want to see her change.

"I had a lot of hate in my heart, but I changed, and people aren't ready to accept that," she says. "For me, it's fine, I always find light in dark times, and I can be a living testimony to someone who changed greatly. When I started receiving all this hate toward me, I understood that I needed to change myself and become positive, and now I meditate, choose to feel good and feel good."

Sony Group Corporation (English: Sony Group Corporation; Japanese: ソニー株式会社) is a multinational Japanese corporation based in the Minato ward of Tokyo. Since April 2018, the company's CEO and president has been Kenichiro Yoshida, and the board chairman is Hiroki Totoki. Sony was founded by Masaru Ibuka and Akio Morita on May 7, 1946 under the name "Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo". The name was eventually changed to Sony in 1958. In 1960, the company established its American subsidiary. During this period, the company began its path as a pioneer in the organizational culture that was prevalent in Japan at that time. For example, company executives were amazed to discover how mobile the employment market was in the United States, and inspired by this, they began to encourage senior executives from competing companies to join Sony. In turn, Sony became an inspiration for other Japanese companies to do the same. During the 1960s, 1970s, and 1980s, Sony was a significant factor in Japan's exports to the United States and was among the major factors in changing the American image of the Japanese market during these decades. Sony's reputation as a company known for quality products helped the company begin selling at prices higher than the prevailing market price.

As a company operating in several areas of a dynamic market like the global technology market, Sony periodically makes various investments in different fields and also reduces various divisions of the company that do not meet their targets. At the beginning of the company's path in the 1940s, it employed 20 workers. Its first product was heating pads. In 1955 the company expanded and began manufacturing transistor radios, and from the 1970s on began making investments in various fields, including the record business. During these decades, it established itself as one of the world's leading companies in photography products, electronics, and more. In 1968, Sony Music Entertainment Japan was founded for activities in the music and entertainment field. In the late 1980s, Sony made several investments in the film industry, purchasing Columbia Records and Columbia Pictures. In the early 1990s, the company entered the video game console market with PlayStation devices developed by the company. In 1995, Aniplex was founded to consolidate the company's activities in the anime field. In January 2006, the Japanese company Minolta announced that it was selling its photography division to Sony. Starting in 2011, Sony began manufacturing smartphones. In April 2012, Sony announced that due to financial difficulties, it would reduce its global workforce by 6%. In February 2014, the company announced a reorganization of the company, including the sale of the VAIO computer division, the privatization of its television division into a private company, and the layoff of 5,000 employees, after the company announced a projected loss of 1.1 billion dollars. On January 25, 2016, Sony acquired the Israeli company Altair for 212 million dollars. At the time of the acquisition, this was the largest deal to date involving the Internet of Things. During the second decade of the 21st century, Sony won achievements and popularity with developments in the field of noise-canceling headphones. On October 10, 2014, Sony intended to hold the premiere of the comedy film "The Interview," whose plot is about two media people sent to interview the ruler of North Korea, Kim Jong-un, and following this, American intelligence agency officials take advantage of it and instruct them on how to assassinate him. Following hackers' threats to Sony Pictures, the film distributor, the company postponed the premiere to December 11 of that year. Initially Sony did not heed the hackers' threats, but after a hacker attack on it, which included among other things terrorist threats like the September 11, 2001 attacks against every movie theater that would screen the film, Sony announced that it would distribute the film for screenings in a limited number of movie theaters. Following Sony's decision, many figures in Hollywood and many fans called Sony's action "cowardly" and said it constitutes a surrender to terrorism and an infringement on freedom of expression. The incident sparked a broad public debate, and Sony, in their defense, argued that limiting the distribution of the film was not their decision, since many movie theater chains decided not to screen the film.

The name Sony was chosen from a combination of the Latin word "sonus" (sound, noise) and the English word "sonny" (son). However, the name "sonney" sounded like "soh-nee" - in Japanese: a failed business, so it was rejected. Also, the owners did not want the company name to have a meaning in every language, so the name "Sony" was chosen. They also chose to register their name in Latin letters instead of traditional Japanese script. At that time, the bank pressured them to be called Sony Electronic Industries or Sony Teletech, but Akio Morita insisted until the bank agreed to register the company under the name SONY.

For years, Sony was a symbol of technological innovation, registering the development of advanced products and technologies such as the world's first transistor radio, the cathode ray tube for televisions, "Trinitron," and the portable Walkman cassette player, alongside other inventions. Sony is still considered today a pioneer and leader in the field of consumer electronics, but equally it is known for its rigidity regarding cooperation with other companies to develop shared standards and for charging substantial sums for licenses to use its developments. This fact led to certain technologies being abandoned despite their technological superiority in favor of technologies from competing companies. The prominent example of this is the format war in the video recording device market. The "Betamax" method developed by Sony was pushed aside in the home market compared to "VHS" developed by JVC, even though VHS was technologically inferior to Betamax. In the last two decades, the company has expanded its activities and turned to content production in addition to the manufacture of electronic devices. During these decades, the company acquired several entertainment companies such as CBS Records and the film studios of "Columbia" and "TriStar". Sony's latest acquisition is MGM studios and their enormous film library. Precisely Sony's new businesses are those from which it has reaped financial satisfaction in recent years, in contrast to the electronics division, which in recent years has suffered heavy losses. In 1995, Aniplex was established to consolidate the company's activities in the anime field. As the company established itself in Japan, Morita and Ibuka wanted their company to be international, so they decided to change the company's name to a name that would be appealing in Western countries. The name Sony was chosen from a combination of the Latin word sonus (sound, voice) and the English word sonny (boy). However, the name sonney sounded like soh-nee - in Japanese: a failing business - and therefore was rejected. Also, the owners did not want the company's name to have a meaning in any language, and thus the name "Sony" was chosen. They also chose to register their name in Latin letters instead of the traditional Japanese script. At the same time, the bank pressured them to call the company Sony Electronic Industries or Sony Teletech, but Akio Morita insisted until the bank agreed to register the company as SONY. This fact led to the abandonment of certain technologies, despite their technological superiority, in favor of technologies from competing companies. The most prominent example of this is the format war in the market for video cassette recorders. The "Betamax" system developed by Sony was pushed aside in the home market compared to "VHS" developed by JVC, even though VHS is technologically inferior to Betamax. In the last two decades, the company has expanded its activities and also turned to content production in addition to the production of electronic devices. The company acquired several entertainment companies during the decades in question, such as the record company CBS and the film studios of "Columbia" and "TriStar". Sony's latest acquisition is MGM Studios and their huge film library. It is Sony's new businesses that have brought it economic satisfaction in recent years compared to the electronics division, which has been suffering heavy losses in recent years. The company's business expansion has caused a conflict of interest between different divisions - the music division did not want the music players of the electronics division to support the MP3 format due to fear of revenue losses, and only recently was such support added to the company's music players due to the roaring successes of competing companies that have taken over the market share that was previously under Sony's control, such as Apple's iPod. In 2016, Sony acquired the Israeli company Altair Semiconductor. The company was founded in 2005, is located in Hod Hasharon, and is engaged in the development of chips for the Internet of Things. Many plants have a dialogue with the animals that eat them, not in spoken language but in shapes and colors designed to catch the eye and stimulate our hunger. To understand how plants speak to us, it's first important to understand what they gain from the deal. When an animal eats a fruit, it takes the fruit's seeds for a ride and "leaves" them somewhere else inside a pile of manure—an excellent starting point for a new plant to sprout. When the fruit's seed has finished developing and is ready for its short journey through the digestive system. ## How Do Fruits Ripen?

Most fruits ripen in response to the plant hormone ethylene. This is a small molecule carried through the air, which is why to speed up the ripening of avocados or bananas, you should put them in a bag with another ripe fruit. Apples are usually picked before they're ripe and stored in a cooled environment with a high percentage of air filtration and carbon dioxide to prevent them from absorbing the ethylene they themselves emit. This way, you can extend their shelf life by months. Sometimes you see an apple that looks as though only half of it has ripened, and in most cases the reason will be partial exposure to ethylene during the ripening process. Not all plants allow you to do this trick, though—wild berries, for example, must ripen on the branch, and if you pick them too early, they'll rot without ripening.

The ripening process begins in the fruit's inner tissue when the seed signals that it's approaching readiness. This way, the seed and the entire fruit ripen together. The fruit becomes sweeter by producing sugars, loses its bitter taste, and softens. In the fruit's skin, the green chlorophyll breaks down, and simultaneously, the plant produces pigments designed to protect the fruit and also give it a more striking hue. These pigments fall into two large groups: carotenoids and anthocyanins, and both groups have striking colors and antioxidant properties that apparently protect the fruit.

Carotenoids are responsible for the red, orange, and yellow colors you can see, for example, in tomatoes and carrots. Carotenoids also give many animals their characteristic color, such as the pink of salmon and flamingos. These animals don't produce carotenoids; they obtain them from their food.

Anthocyanins are responsible for the red, purple, and blue colors you can see in plants like raspberries, blueberries, black beans, and red cabbage.
